DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Terminable services-
538. Freight assistance on western feed grains- further amount required, $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: This item represents underestimating by the government as to the amount of feed grain that would be qualifying for this subsidy during the current fiscal year. We find that the amount previously provided is not sufficient. There has been no change in the policy, of course, and none is suggested by this supplementary item, but it does mean that during this fiscal year we will have paid a greater amount by way of subsidy on feed grain than at any time during recent memory, and the full amount of $2 million is needed now in order to make these payments.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to criticize the payment of this freight assistance in any way, but to criticize the administration in so far as the red tape, etc., that has to be gone through is concerned and the fact the government has never made this a permanent policy as we have requested on many occasions in this house. The uncertainty with regard to this freight assistance has made it necessary for eastern feeders to avoid dependence on western grain for their feed requirements. It is for this reason that eastern feeders have probably increased their acreage of corn to a greater extent than would have been necessary had there been some stability in government policy with respect to freight assistance.
We never know when it is going to be dropped. It has been hinted on various occasions that the measure would be dropped. The farmer is never sure. We have asked on

several occasions that more storage space be made available for western feed grain and this has been promised. However, we are not sure whether or not it has been made available and on many occasions it has been difficult for eastern feeders to be sure of the quantity of western feed grain available.
I want to point out that this has been called, by certain people, a straight subsidy to eastern feeders. It is no such thing. It does enable the western producer to dispose of some of his surplus to eastern feeders in a great deal better way than he could if this freight assistance were not paid. The advantage, I think, it could be fairly said, is just about 50-50 between the western producer and the eastern feeder. If there is any truth in the fact the government is considering eliminating this policy then I wish they would come out and say so. As I say, there is no certainty in the mind of the eastern feeder as to whether the assistance will be continued. He cannot make his plans very far ahead, so he adopts the only other course-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Did my hon. friend not see the estimates that were placed before us the other day?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I saw that, but tomorrow the government could say they were not going to pay it next year; that is what I am trying to bring out. We have asked on various occasions that this be made a permanent policy so the farmer would know what to expect from one year to the next. A man cannot change the rotation of his crops in two weeks. He cannot decide he is going to put in double the acreage of feed grain in two weeks. He has to plan ahead. If the government is not considering eliminating this assistance, then at least tell the eastern feeder what the policy of the government is. It has been clearly indicated to us today by the answers to the questions on the orders of the day that the government is continuing to consider matters but makes no firm statement as to what they are considering or what their decisions have been.
As I said before, as a consequence of this uncertainty eastern farmers have increased their acreage of corn and that is detrimental to the western producer because naturally if the eastern feeder is producing more corn then he is not going to require the amount of western feed grain he would otherwise require. Then, there is the matter of price which has caused some eastern feeders to hesitate about purchasing western feed grain. There are many uncertainties in connection with this system. As I said, we have urged the government to make this legislation permanent in nature. I hope the government will state now that the policy will be in effect
Supply-Agriculture
for another year at least if they do not want to make it permanent, so the farmers can plan now for their future requirements.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, that the government has not listened to the vociferous pleas on the part of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre for the abolition of freight assistance on feed grain.
I am very pleased to know his is a voice crying in the wilderness in this respect. I trust that in respect to old age pensions, the difficulties from which we have been suffering and many other questions he has raised, his will continue to be a voice crying in the wilderness. We are pleased to know that the policy of the government is to continue this freight assistance. It is of great help to the farmers in British Columbia, particularly the dairy and poultry producers because the cost of grain is a major item in their costs.
I do urge the government to give reconsideration to the restoring of the reduction that was given effect last year, because this assistance is paid on the basis of so much per ton and every time there is a freight rate increase, from which the farmers have suffered recently, the percentage of assistance they receive in respect of this feed grain is lessened and lessened. I urge that consideration be given to that, particularly in view of the recent freight rate increases across Canada.
I have the honour to represent, on the whole, small farmers who work long hours and who receive a very modest return, but their costs are high with respect to feed grains. There is one community that is now paying $80 per ton for No. 5 wheat landed on the wharf at that point, and that is the highest cost of which I know at the present time. Then, the farmer has to truck it 20 miles in some cases. When you relate that cost to the farmer to what the wheat producers on the prairie are receiving you can see that someone in between is pinching quite a lot and it is the opinion of the farmers I have the honour to represent that it is the milling companies of Canada.
Now, because of that situation which has existed over quite a number of years there is a growing demand on the part of dairy and poultry producers in my constituency for the government to make arrangements to enable them to buy their wheat or grain direct from the farmer through the wheat board and overcome this middleman's cost. Our farmers are organized members of fruit associations, poultry organizations and dairy organizations, and they would not for a moment want to do anything that would destroy the effective organization with respect to the marketing of wheat on the prairies. But we do suggest that the government could give consideration

Supp ly-A griculture
to making some arrangements for these producers to buy in carload lots direct from the farmers through the wheat board and overcome this middleman's cost. That is all I have to say on this question, at the present time, Mr. Chairman. In conclusion, I once again urge the government to reconsider the amount of the subsidy in view of the recent increase in freight costs.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: We, in this group, have always supported the policy of freight assistance on feed grains to both the east and the west. I agree with the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand that there should be a greater degree of permanence given to this legislation so the farmers would know this policy will continue and they can plan ahead. I have one or two questions I should like to ask in this regard. Can the minister say what was the total amount of freight assistance given on shipments to both the east and the west? Can the minister break down both of those amounts to show how much was for oats, how much for barley and how much for wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I can give the total over a number of years of the payments made with respect to the shipments in all the provinces, but the details as to how it is broken down in the various kinds of grain I could not give. I can only add that I notice it comes to some $254 million over the period of time that the subsidy has been in effect. This year the increase is expected to be something in the order of 200,000 tons more than last year, but I will put on the record by way of answers to questions the information requested. As to the permanent side of it, I might draw to the attention of the committee that I am afraid I am entering into a discussion of next year's estimates. The reason I intervened when the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand was speaking is that the provision is in this year's estimates again.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I assume the government is not responsible for the quality of feed grain sold under this legislation. When the hon. member for Kootenay West was speaking he must have drawn to the attention of the committee whether or not the government should subsidize the freight charges upon rubbish such as certainly is received sometimes by the farmers in the maritime provinces. I do not know whether I should say this, but I think there is a distinct connection between the subsidization of freight and the quality of the material that is shipped to the eastern provinces. I am well aware of the fact that a good deal of the mixing is done in the provinces. I personally have seen what was supposed to be feed grain put out by private mixers in one of the

maritime provinces and I saw a farmer in one of those provinces mix some of the so-called feed with water and offer it to his hogs. They refused to eat it.
I think I might add a word on what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said. I have mentioned this before. Apparently it is not a good idea because nobody ever does anything about it. It seems to me that when there is a feed industry of such great volume as they have in the maritime provinces the farmers should get together in their cooperatives and buy grain, as my colleague suggested, not necessarily from the western farmers through the wheat board but from the wheat board itself. I do not care whom they buy it from, but I think it should be bought under a Canadian certificate of quality so that those people would know what they are getting.
I am well aware of the fact that a great deal of this mixing is done by private concerns. There is a great bulk of wheat seeds, rubbish, wild oats, wild buckwheat and other grains of that kind that disappear every year. They go somewhere. My suspicion is that they go into the stomachs of maritime hogs.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I want to say just a word on this problem raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West. The interest of the farmers in my constituency in the question of feed grain arises mainly in respect of the cattle ranchers who wish to put their cattle on grain to finish them for market. Our area is not a good grain-growing area but it is a very good cattle-ranching area. The situation is that we are in direct competition with prairie beef on the British Columbia market. The British Columbia ranching industry does not produce more than from 40 per cent to 45 per cent of the beef consumed in our province. The rest is brought in mainly from Calgary and Edmonton, but most of it from Calgary. Therefore, it will be seen that in our own domestic market we compete with prairie beef, probably 100 per cent of which is grain-fed. When we pay the prices for our feed grain, which the hon. member for Kootenay West referred to, it will be seen that we are at a very distinct disadvantage, particularly in light of the fact that the fashion being set now is almost universally for grain-fed beef. We know that well-finished, grass-fed beef is just as good as grain-fed beef, but we are a minority producing province and it is virtually impossible to fight against the trend for feed-grain beef which is set by the packers. Something has to be done. Either the feed-grain assistance must be increased or else our

ranchers must be allowed to buy direct from the farms on the prairies their supplies of feed-grain, as the prairie farmer is allowed to do now. It may be that it would have to be a combination of both.
The prairie farmer gets his feed grain at about $20 or $25 a ton from his neighbour without any interference. We are not allowed to buy it direct from the farm and if we do we do not get any feed grain assistance in bringing it in and so we are hit both ways. It is an economic problem of great proportions for our farmers. I am not speaking for an area that is not really a good beef-producing area; I am speaking for an area that is a good beef-producing area, as the Minister of Agriculture knows, but which is squeezed between the two policies of the government, one of which seeks to reduce the feed grain assistance per ton, while the other makes it impossible for the farmers to buy their grain at prices which will enable them to compete with their competitors on the prairies. If the policy of not permitting direct farm purchases is to be followed, then I think the only fair thing to do-and I insist the only fair thing to do-is to increase the amount of feed grain assistance so that our farmers will be relieved by that action from the consequences of the unfair competitive position they are placed in by the other action of the government.
Since we are discussing this question of feed grain assistance, this seems to me to be the appropriate place to bring it up. The Minister of Finance apparently is in charge of putting these supplementary estimates through. I put it to him, and he has the choice, in fairness, of increasing the amount provided for feed grain assistance or persuading his colleagues to permit us to buy grain direct from the prairies.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I would be remiss in my duties if I failed to take part in this particular discussion by reason of the fact that some of the questions raised are of relative importance to the district which I represent.
I feel, as do other hon. members, that the feed grain assistance must be maintained. I was very interested in the observations made by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand because I recall that on April 9 last year, I think it was, when the board of transport commissioners held their hearings in respect of freight rates, a portion of a letter from the Minister of Agriculture was read in which he was purported to have written that there is of course a possibility parliament might change the law.
As I recall it, about February 28, 1954,- I have not the Hansard here-when this same 82715-42
Supply-Agriculture
minister brought in a change in the regulations which drastically reduced feed grain assistance to my province, it had a dire effect upon the industry in the lower mainland of British Columbia.
I fully realize that what the Minister of Finance said is quite true-and I think he would agree with me-that when a certain figure appears in the estimates it does not necessarily follow that it will be used. If the government decides that the regulations are going to be changed, then we can have such a change and it can have a marked effect upon our industry in British Columbia. The fact remains that agriculture is the third most important primary industry in British Columbia, second to logging and mining. It does play a very important part in our lives.
With respect to the question raised by the hon. member for Kamloops, I would draw to his attention and to the attention of the committee that possibly the answer is not entirely in the fact that we have this feed grain assistance that he mentioned.
I hold in my hand a clipping from the Manitoba Co-operator of June 21, 1956, which would indicate that the complaint of one Stephen Francis Murphy, a turkey farmer from Mission, British Columbia, was heard by the courts and the following judgment was handed down:
Had the plaintiff transported his own grain from Manitoba to British Columbia for his own use, I question whether the prohibition would apply. Here the plaintiff purchased grain in Manitoba and tendered it for shipment to a company in British Columbia.
The fact remains that a British Columbia farmer is not permitted to buy grain from any of the prairie provinces without having it go through the wheat board. I am not opposed to that. I feel the wheat board is doing an excellent job in this country and I would like to see it retained. However, the difficulty as I see it is summed up in this article from the Financial Post of December 10, 1955. I realize that the date is old but it has a significant bearing on this matter. Under a dateline from Lethbridge, Alberta the article says:
At the 90 cent level, feedlot operators were swamped with deliveries of high-grade wheat. Many bought enough grain to maintain feeding operations for two years.
The farmers in Alberta and Manitoba can exchange grain at any price they wish and for considerably less than what we pay in British Columbia. The article continues:
I have just sold 10,000 bushels of No. 2 wheat at 60 cents a bushel not because I need the cash but rather because I don't see any hope of selling all my grain to the wheat board within the next two years.

Supply-Agriculture
Compare that with the minimum price the British Columbia farmer pays for No. 5 wheat of about $3 a hundredweight.
There we have a specific instance of what is being done on the prairies. I do not blame the prairie farmers. They have to get ready cash and this is a common-sense way of carrying on business, but why should they be denied the right of sending grain into British Columbia on that same basis? Better still, why should the British Columbia livestock and poultry producer be denied the right of purchasing grain on the same basis as does any farmer on the prairies? If the price is going to be consistent they should all pay the same price. We have the awkward position spoken of by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson wherein farmers in his area who raise a great deal of feed grain find it impossible to send their grain into the British Columbia market because merchants in British Columbia find it to their advantage to import birds and other products from the United States. We are not only denying a proper market to the British Columbia producers but we are also denying the prairie farmers the right to send grain into that area. I would therefore strongly urge the minister to consider a further supplementary estimate in this respect in the forthcoming year to bring back into effect the $5 that he removed on February 28, 1954.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to endorse a great deal that has already been said particularly by the hon. member for Saskatoon who complained of the quality of the grains that are being sold in markets as feed. I saw a sample not long ago which I am sure consisted mainly of sweepings and dust. It was totally unfit to be put on the market for sale and I think the minister should carefully consider the type of feed that is receiving the subsidy; otherwise we are encouraging a trade that is of no credit to Canada through shipping such grain.
I would also urge support for what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay West regarding dairy and poultry producers being able to bring their own grain from the prairies. In my area we have several retired wheat farmers who are now engaged in fruit growing and from them I have learned that if they want to get grain from their own farms on the prairies it cannot be done directly, nor can they ship their own fruit from British Columbia to the district on the prairies where they formerly lived because that is forbidden and so they must have a middleman and the railway companies each taking a pound of flesh out of both products in which the farmers are interested.

The result of this is that on the prairie a farmer has to sell five bushels of grain to buy a basket of apples and in the Okanagan valley he must sell five baskets of apples to buy a bushel of grain. The whole situation is stupid and the intervening red tape which causes this discrepancy in the cost of moving the products should be removed. I feel that the assistance now given is completely inadequate, but over and above an increase in the assistance some step should be taken to make it possible for a farmer who formerly lived on the prairies, and who is now interested in doing so, to bring in feed grain he cannot sell from his own farm to British Columbia through the wheat board but not through other channels. I think much could be done to help the prairie farmers dispose of their feed grain and the poultry and dairy farmers of British Columbia to take advantage of a fair price for their commodities.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman* I appreciate the difficulties of the farmers on the mainland of British Columbia but those difficulties are quite small compared with the problem which faces the poultry men on Vancouver island because not only do they have to pay freight by rail but there are the additional charges to move the feed from the mainland to Vancouver island.
As is well known, owing to the skill of the breeders on Vancouver island a strain of turkeys has been developed which is sometimes referred to as the double-breasted bronze which are now accepted all across Canada, and the entire turkey business very largely depends on the ability of the Vancouver island breeders to produce enough eggs to sell the day-old poults to the breeders in other parts of the country.
I feel that the business of the legitimate feed merchants should be protected because while it may be possible for some of the larger farmers to purchase feed direct from farmers in Alberta or Saskatchewan nevertheless the majority of the small farmers will not buy in carload lots and will have to deal through regular grain merchants. From the information I have received from grain merchants on Vancouver island I am convinced that their margin of profit is extremely small. It would seem to me that the solution to this problem would be to restore the freight assistance to the amount it was a few years ago before the reductions were unfortunately made. I do hope that in the coming year it will be possible for the government to increase freight assistance over the amount that is now being provided.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say on this particular item not because I am a farming expert but because

I am taking a look at the economics of this proposition. In the main estimates there is a provision for $16,500,000 for feed grain assistance.
The minister is realistically stepping them up $3 million more this year. That is quite a bill and it is accumulating from year to year. As I see it the questions of feed grain and fertilizer are interlocked; they go together.
I do not see any reason why the maritime provinces should not supply themselves with feed grain provided they are given the necessary assistance, particularly with respect to obtaining fertilizer for the purpose of rehabilitating their land. I think it is time that we began to think of that. The other place is establishing a committee to look into the question of better uses of land and the Gordon commission also emphasizes that matter.
During the war, I think around 1942, the department of munitions and supply made a grant to the Dominion Coal Company for the purpose of research into the use of the slag at the steel plant as a fertilizer. Quite a lot of money was spent on that. I do not know whether or not a report was made by the company. However, a few weeks ago an eminent agricultural expert in the maritimes made the statement that there were 100,000 tons of slag being thrown away each year at that steel plant which could have been used as fertilizer on the land in Nova Scotia.
It is costing a lot of money to take feed grain from the prairies into the maritimes. I think that the cost down there is about $80 a ton; it is $60 in British Columbia. I know that fertilizer is well over $90 a ton. The point I am making is that this assistance is necessary in the unplanned use of our land at the present time. I do not think that the answer is just in continuing to give assistance but is also in what the Senate committee will find and what the Gordon commission will find as to better utilization of our land in our own area. I believe that the questions of fertilizer and feed grain are interlocked. I might tell the minister that in my lifetime we had one of the largest fertilizer plants in Canada located at that steel plant in Sydney. It was there until the late thirties but it followed the other industries into Canada. Now we are dragging it back and paying subsidies on feed grain and other commodities which we think could be produced in the maritime provinces for our own use at least.
I wish to leave this observation with the minister because it is true, at least I think it is, that there is 100,000 tons of slag which could be used as fertilizer and thereby provide fertilizer cheaply if not gratis to the farmers in that area, which would assist them 82715-42i

Mr. Chairman, there is a point or two which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and also to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture regarding assistance with respect to feed grain. I believe since the main estimates on this were passed during the last year there has been an increase in freight rates, and this has had a very detrimental effect on the economy on using feed grains from the west in the maritimes in spite of the assistance, because as has already been pointed out by some hon. members, especially the member for Kootenay West and the member for Humber-St. George's, in the throne speech debate, and I would commend him on what he had to say to the minister, by reason of the 11 per cent increase in freight rates the freight cost of delivering a ton of grain in the maritimes has increased, depending upon the area, as much as 50 per cent of what it previously cost.
As a result of a whole series of freight rate increases since this legislation was first introduced much of its benefit has been dissipated because the actual cost per ton in freight on feed grain brought into the maritimes has increased. It has gone up rapidly, I believe, because there has been no corresponding increase in the amount granted by the feed grain assistance legislation. I would like to have some information from the minister as to what is the actual freight rate cost of delivering a ton of grain to some representative point in the maritimes, and also what it was when this legislation was first introduced, what it is now and perhaps what it was at an intermediate point when the freight rates were at some intermediate figure. In any case this rapid increase in freight rates on feed grain to the maritimes has in many instances made the difference between a profitable and an unprofitable operation in the case of persons who are producing pork, turkeys and many other things. The result now is that many farmers in the maritimes have gone completely out of pork production because of the increased cost of feed.
For the last couple of years in the maritimes we have had the absurd situation that when a woman goes into a meat shop, especially during the holiday season, to buy a turkey she is as likely as not to get a turkey which was raised in California or in some other large turkey ranch in the United States. Part of the reason why these imports are increasing is that they are more highly processed and in most cases are ready for the oven when bought; frequently that is not the case with respect to Canadian turkeys.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to support some of the things that have

been said here with regard to the position of dairy and poultry farmers on the coast. There are quite a large number of poultry farmers in my constituency, and they suffer very badly from the effects of the present price structure with regard to feed. Some of them have, I think, been overcoming their difficulties recently by bringing in feed grain from the Peace river block of British Columbia which they can do, of course, without interference by the wheat board authorities.
However, I think there are certain disadvantages about that type of solution. In the first place I do not think we should rely on records which might undermine the position of the wheat board and, in the second place, the supply of feed grain from the Peace river block is fairly limited; they don't get a subsidy. It has occurred to me for some time, Mr. Chairman, that we are overlooking a very useful natural advantage that we have in western Canada. We have on the Pacific coast the only temperate climate in Canada-the only mild climate.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: What about ours?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
It is merely a matter of meteorological fact, and because this is a matter of meteorological fact it means that on the Pacific coast the production of dairy and poultry products can be undertaken in much more advantageous circumstances than it can in more severe climates. We have on the other side of the Rockies one of the major grain-growing areas of the world, and it does seem strange to me, Mr. Chairman, that we have not yet achieved some arrangement of our agricultural economy in this country whereby the enormous stocks of feed grain for which, according to my colleagues here, the prairie farmers receive the very minimum of income, cannot be transported to the Pacific coast for use in the manufacture of dairy and poultry products under the very best conditions.
I admit that this is not entirely due to the operations of the government, but it is perhaps due in part to the failure of the government to take action. In British Columbia almost the entire feed business is under the control of two firms; one is a wholly-owned subsidiary of one of the large milling companies of Canada, and the other has a close connection with a milling company by virtue of interlocking directorships. The "spread" between the price paid to the producers of grain and the price paid by my constituents is almost unbelievable, and as an instance of this robbery that is going on I would like to cite the case of one of my constituents who has a very large turkey

farm. He decided one day that he was "fed up" with the enormous price the feed company was charging for grain, so the next time the salesman for that company came round he said he was making arrangements to bring grain from the Peace river, and instal his own grinding machinery. The salesman promptly reduced the price by $17 a ton.
The government did institute an investigation, some years ago, of this particular factor in our economy-the milling industry-and some quite startling revelations came out of that inquiry, but no action was taken at that time. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that while the subsidy on grain feeds is certainly desirable and, as the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke said just now, should be increased, that in itself will not solve the main problem, which is to see that the produce of the prairie farmers reaches the people in my constituency and province who need it, paying the least possible tribute to the middleman in the process.
I would commend to the Minister of Agriculture that he undertake a very careful restudy of that hearing which was held with regard to the milling and grain industry a few years ago, and consider whether or not there are some steps he could advise his colleagues to take in order to remedy this fantastic situation in which a stable and profitable dairy and poultry industry on the Pacific coast is being hamstrung year after year owing to this enormous "spread" between the price paid to the prairie producer and the price paid by	poultry
and dairy nroaucers on the coast. I think this is a matter of urgent national importance, and some steps should be taken by the government to remedy the present situation.

Mr. Chairman, I have spoken on this and similar matters on several occasions in the past, and therefore I propose to speak for only a moment or two now. I want to say again what I have stressed in the past, namely that this is not to be considered in any way as a "handout", or as assistance to something which does not give a definite economic return to the Dominion of Canada. I am quite certain that of all the expenditures made by this government in all phases of activity there is none which has produced a greater economic return than this, or helped more, in our area, to increase the gross national product to which the Minister of Finance is so pleased to refer.
We have developed in the east today an agriculture industry which is dependent
Supp ly-A gricu Iture
almost entirely on this freight rate subvention. In the county of Kings, in my constituency, we have one of the largest poultryraising areas in Canada. A few years ago it was on a deficiency basis. Only the day before yesterday one of the leaders in the establishment of that industry, Mr. Manning Ells, the largest producer of day-old chicks in Canada, and the man who founded the poultry industry in that whole area, died. It was due to his leadership, to a large extent, that the poultry industry grew as it has done.
I want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that this matter of a subsidy is vital. Secondly, I join with others who have spoken in believing that in view of the increase of freight rates which has taken place the government should give consideration to increasing the subsidy; whether or not that can be done at present is a matter of government policy, but certainly the speeches made in this house indicate the necessity of such action. It does not do a man much good to receive a subsidy which met the case a few years ago; today we are confronted by a continued horizontal increase in freight rates until the benefit of any subsidy received has been largely wiped out. It would be interesting to know the position of the producers in the maritimes today with regard to the effect of this subsidy as compared with their position before this horizontal increase in the freight rates came into operation.
Again I want to urge that the time has come when this should be made a permanent part of government fiscal policy. The hon. member for Brant-Haldimand asked this morning if there was any truth in reports that this scheme might be discontinued. The Minister of Finance, of course, can say:	Well,
look at your estimates. But as the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand pointed out, the estimates are only for this year, and even then we are not sure whether they are going to be adopted or whether the money is going to be spent.
At its recent convention the party to which I belong adopted as one of its planks that this policy should be a part of the permanent economic policy of the Dominion of Canada. It is not fair to producers who have risked their savings, who have developed the industry as they have and have turned a deficit area into a surplus one as they have in the east, to be dependent on the vagaries of a government to determine whether they are going to include X dollars for the subsidy this year or whether they are going to include Y dollars or whether they are not going to include anything. Then too, up until recently at least, we

Supply-Agriculture
have had half of the amount voted in the main estimates and the other half voted in the supplementaries.
This is one of the most important things which has been done for agriculture in eastern Canada in the last 20 years. It is justified in every way, shape and form. It has returned more money to the Dominion of Canada than any other one expenditure made for agriculture in the east. I am sure that no government would think of doing away with it, but let us have it written into the law in such a form that the producers can go ahead with some certainty. They face enough difficulties today without having to wonder about the whims and caprices of this government or any government that might be in power, and the time has come when this scheme should be made permanent.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I have a question. I should like to ask the minister to clarify the problem to which the hon. member for Nanaimo referred. If a co-operative in British Columbia, Ontario or the maritimes were desirous of making a purchase of grain from a farmer in western Canada, would the subsidy be granted? I know that they would have to make the paper arrangement of having the grain sold to the Canadian wheat board and then in turn purchasing it from the board. However, can a co-operative or a large farmer buy a carload of wheat from a western farmer through the channels of the Canadian wheat board and still receive the subsidy on that carload of grain? Suppose someone-it might even be someone with a large turkey ranch as the hon. member for Nanaimo said-wanted to buy a carload of No. 6 wheat from a farmer in Saskatchewan who had a large enough quota to fill a car. Could he make arrangements with the wheat board to buy that car from the farmer, have the car shipped directly to him and purchase it from the wheat board and receive the subsidy on that carload of grain?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been suggested that I might say something on this matter and one or two other matters that have been mentioned. I had hoped that I would discuss these matters on the general estimates of my department which deal with these different problems. This item only deals with one thing and I do not think we are completely in order in discussing quite a number of other things. This item only has to do with assistance on freight.
The question which has just been raised is one which does involve the farmer in some difficulties but at the same time it is very difficult to see how it can be otherwise if we are going to have the wheat board system.

The legislation that we have goes just as far as we can go under the constitution. We can control the passing of grain over a provincial boundary line and we do that under the wheat board act, but when it comes to moving grain within a province we are not able to control that.
That results in some of the things that have been mentioned, the first one being that according to a letter that was written one farmer had sold wheat to another at 60 cents a bushel, and the suggestion is that he ought to be able to sell it from one province into another at 60 cents a bushel. I have said before and I am going to repeat that is something that can be corrected by the prairie governments. It should not be permissible for a farmer or feed dealer to take advantage of a farmer who is in difficulties because he cannot get cash to induce him to accept 60 cents a bushel for wheat that is worth $1.40 even on the basis of the advance payment. There is only one authority that can stop that and that is the provincial authority. I suggest to some of my friends opposite who have been doing considerable talking that they have far more influence with these governments than I have.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Why do you not answer the question?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I suggest that they use their influence. I am answering the question which you were talking about out in the west a while ago and you will be talking about it again.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: When?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The suggestion is that because wheat was sold in Alberta by one farmer to another at 60 cents a bushel it should be possible to sell it over the boundary line into British Columbia at 60 cents a bushel from one farmer to another. I do not think it should be possible in a province on the western plains for wheat to be sold at 60 cents a bushel within that province when that wheat, even on the basis of the advance payment, has a value of $1.40 a bushel. That is something that can only be dealt with by the provincial governments.
With respect to the other question of moving wheat through the wheat board, it stands to reason that when the wheat is put into the elevator then no matter which elevator it is the farmer gets an advance payment and he also has the right to get interim payments and the final payment when they are made. Therefore he is not only entitled to the initial payment when the wheat goes into the elevator but to full final payment.
The wheat board insists that the wheat remain in position to obtain when it is sold to

the purchaser and no matter where it is sold the price which can be obtained at the time it is sold. Therefore what is actually said is that you can put wheat into an elevator of a certain elevator company or one of the pool elevators and it can .be shipped over the mountains into British Columbia or shipped elsewhere and then you can get the wheat from the wheat board out of the elevator of that same company. It may not be exactly the same wheat. I do not suppose they can follow it through. Having taken it into the elevator at the initial point, it would be difficult to declare that it was exactly the same wheat but it would be wheat of the same grade, and it could be purchased on the other side of the mountains at whatever price the board is selling wheat on that particular day.
That money comes back into the pool and there is provision for interim payments and a final payment. If we are going to have the wheat board system I do not know how it can be done in any other way in order to make absolutely certain that the farmer on the one side of the mountains gets his proper initial payment and the farmer on the other side pays whatever the current price is at the particular time he takes it out. Therefore the whole thing enters into the transactions in connection with the pool that is carried on by the wheat board, and that is possible at present and can be done.
One or two other questions were raised during the discussion which I think I should mention while I am on my feet. One had to do with the quality of the feed which a person in the maritimes purchases or the quality of the feed on the other side of the mountains. I have continually before me on my desk in my office a list of the prices of feed for chicks on the other side of the mountains. One of the very big costs involved in those prices is fish meal which certainly is not produced on the prairies. It is produced right near where the chickens are fed. In addition, other parts of the cost are ingredients which are not involved in these freight payments at all. It is only the grain that is involved in that, and it is not grain as it is ground into feed even down in the maritime provinces or in Ontario, but it is the wheat, oats and barley that is shipped and the freight is paid on it. Then, some feed merchant in one or the other of the provinces takes that grain and has it ground into feed which is sold to the farmer. It is quite a different product from the product on which the freight assistance is paid initially.
I am quite sure that hon. members will agree too that when you put that ground feed, even if nothing else is in it but wheat,
Supply-Agriculture
oats and barley, if you put it into a bag and have the bag all handsomely painted up, there is a considerable part of the cost which the farmer is paying which is not related to the grain but is related to some service. I quite understand my hon. friend from British Columbia indicating that all the farmer had to do when he was talking to the feed merchant was to point out he could ship the grain from the Peace river area down to where he was at a certain price in order to get the tonnage price of the finished product reduced by $17. Again, I call attention to the fact that is a transaction entirely within the province of British Columbia. This government has nothing to do with it whatever.

speechtext: You will not pay feed grain assistance on it?

speechtext:
Of course, we do not; we do not within any province. We do not pay freight assistance on the movement of grain produced within a province to some other place within the province. As my hon. friend has said, the farmer can go to the feed merchant and say: Here I can get that grain from the Peace river country shipped down at such a rate and I can grind it myself. The feed merchant naturally does not want the farmer to get into that practice. Every farmer can do that. He can send over to the prairies and get it through the wheat board method at a much lower rate than he is being charged by the man who ground the feed, but the feed merchants do not want him to do that. This is merely a matter of bargaining between the individual on the one hand and the feed man on the other. The whole transaction is carried out within the province, and if there is any regulation of it required it would be done by the province.
I repeat that while it would probably cost a little more to get it over the mountains into Vancouver than it does to get it down from the Peace river country, or perhaps it is vice versa, I do not know, but whatever the difference is there is far more than that added in many of these instances referred to by other costs that have nothing to do with freight rates on the shipment of grain. I would suggest again, therefore, that many of these questions could be better discussed when we get around to my estimates, at which time they could be discussed under the different items to which they belong.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words about item No. 538, whereby we are asked to vote an extra $2 million for assistance to western feed grain transport. My purpose will be to point out the benefits derived from the act authorizing that assistance, particularly as it concerns Quebec farmers and feeders.
As is known, that assistance dates from October, 1941, and involves the payment by the federal government of a substantial part of the freight costs of grain shipped from the Fort William elevators eastward, notably to Montreal and Saint John, N.B., with additional compensations for other intermediate marketing centres.
Quebec farmers count on western grain. In fact 75 per cent of the feed grain consumed in that province comes from the prairies. That means that more than a million tons of grain are brought each year from the west to Quebec. I hope that hon. members from

Supply-Agriculture
the prairies are grateful for this Quebec patronage of grain producers in western Canada.
The high cost of these grains at the shipping point and the equally high cost of transportation have become a problem for Quebec farmers and cattle producers because of the rise in the operating costs of their farms and of the low selling price of their products.
Since October, 1941, the federal government has paid the not inconsiderable amount of $102 million in subsidies for the transportation of this grain from Fort William to the various selling points in the province of Quebec, the amount shipped as of December 1, 1956 being 15,633,000 tons. The average subsidy per ton has been $6.52 between 1941 and 1953 and since 1953, $7.98 per ton.
Quebec farmers and cattle breeders have therefore benefited from an average annual subsidy of $7,259,100, according to the terms of this useful piece of legislation.
It is estimated that it takes 1,000 pounds, that is half a ton of feed, to get an average hog ready for slaughtering. It therefore means that our farmers have received an average of about $4 per hog under the freight subsidy on feed grain. Without that subsidy which brings more than seven million dollars to Quebec, and without the premiums on quality, which bring an average of $1,226,100 a year to the farmers and breeders of Quebec, this kind of breeding would have come to an end long ago, in my opinion. So the Quebec farmers are in a position to appreciate the generosity of the federal government.
I am therefore pleased, as the representative of the farmers of Roberval constituency, to congratulate the federal government on its policy with regard to grain transport and I ask them to maintain and, if possible, to increase that subsidy to the greatest benefit of our farmers who are now going through difficult times.
The farmers of my constituency, as a result of the poor crop in 1956, will have to apply outside for seed grain, and I know that this legislation providing assistance to the transportation of grain will help them indirectly to face that new ordeal.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I should ask this house to accept this item without giving a brief explanation, not only as to what is being asked for but also what is being done as a result of the policies which received almost universal approval in the house at the special session in November.
As hon. members will recall, the day after the session was prorogued I left for Vienna. I arrived in Vienna on the following day and remained there for three days. In spite of the fact that one or two newspapers in this country questioned whether it was necessary or even useful for me to make that journey, I think that if we intended to carry on the policy which was explained and approved here in parliament it was a good thing for me to have done, because it was possible to decide on the spot certain things which would have been difficult for officials to decide on the spot, which would have required a great deal of communication and clarification for someone who was a long distance away. One of the things which was in my mind and which I thought might cause difficulty before I went to Austria was that we might not have enough real estate to deal adequately with the problem. I had on one or two occasions impressed this point on my officials.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Real estate?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
