I said real estate and I meant real estate, premises in which people could sit down while waiting for applications to be dealt with. Our office in Vienna is, as are all our offices, maintained as
662	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration economically as possible. This office happens to be on the fourth or fifth floor, or on both floors of an office building in Vienna in which there is a small lift which will carry about two people and a stairway going around the lift, which is fine if you have six or seven people going into a building in an hour. On the Monday morning after I arrived in Vienna there were over 100 people at the door of that building, I was informed, at five o'clock in the morning; I was not there but I was told. At the time I was finishing my breakfast at the hotel, at about nine o'clock, the manager of our office came to see me and said, I do not think that you ought to make your visit to the office for a while yet because it is impossible to get into the building, the stairways are jammed, the lift is jammed and it is impossible to move.
I said that this was really exactly what I expected. I felt that the real problem would not be a lack of personnel and probably not even a lack of doctors nor a lack of transport to bring the people to Canada, but that the real problem would be a lack of space in which to deal with applicants. I said that I thought there was every reason why I should go at once to examine the situation. In the meantime the police had persuaded the people to move back so that it was possible to enter the building. We immediately got in touch by telephone with someone who had a dance hall or a similar building a few miles away which had been used by a shipping company to make arrangements for the transport of a group of Hungarians who were coming to Canada later. I said that this place should be rented for the rest of the month. We finally managed to get hold of somebody who had some authority over the place and told him we were coming along in a car to take over and that we would discuss the rent afterwards. By 11.30 our officials were actually processing people in that building, having hired two or three buses to bring them a couple of miles across the town from the regular office to this place.
The same difficulties occurred with respect to having a staging point where these people could wait until transport was available to bring them to Canada. There was also the problem of getting shipping space. We had an airlift which of course was very helpful in getting some people moving quickly, but to move any large numbers it was obviously preferable to have shipping. Mr. Jacobsen from the inter-governmental committee on European migration came to Vienna and met me at noon on that Monday and we made arrangements right there and then for enough ships for about 5,000 Hungarians.


During the course of the morning, just before lunch, I had seen the Austrian minister of the interior for half an hour and had sought to impress upon him the importance of making one camp available in Austria for people who were coming to Canada so that they could be kept together, and so that they would be available, and we would know where they were when the transport was available. Of course, this camp was not to have been run by the Canadian government and it was not even originally thought that it would be operated by Canadians at all. It was to be under the general charge of ICEM, if I may abbreviate the rather long name of that organization, and we were told the barracks at Wiener Neustadt might be made available. Incidentally, I understand these were the barracks where Marshal Tito many years ago did his military training when he was in the army of the Austrian empire.
This place had been left rather a shambles by the Russians. I insisted on going out to see it. I had been told that it was all ready to receive people, that it had beds, mattresses, a kitchen and other essentials. Well, there were a few beds and a few straw mattresses. There were no windows and there was no heating. I had been told there was a kitchen but nobody could find the key to the door. It was pretty clear that it would take quite a lot of elementary rehabilitation before people could be put in it at all in very cold weather, and it was cold. We did get things in train to get that done and it was occupied about ten days later.
It did not seem to me, after that, that there was much more I could usefully do in Vienna; because ihy experience is that ministers are all very well in their way, but once questions of policy are settled it is very much better to leave the officials alone to get on with the work instead of remaining under foot.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Better for the minister to get out of the way.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Well, I got out of the way.
This story has been told before in other places, but I think I should like to place it on Hansard. When I arrived in Vienna on Saturday afternoon, one of the first things I was told was that there was a faculty of forestry of one of the Hungarian universities which had come in toto across the boundary into Austria and that the dean of the faculty had approached our ambassador a day or two before to discuss with him the possibility of their coming to Canada. I must say that this rather fired my imagination, and during the evening while I was dining with the Austrian foreign minister I kept thinking of

this faculty and how it could be dealt with and dealt with expeditiously.
Finally, late that evening I sent a telegram to my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries, and a telegram to my wife asking my wife to telephone me at an hour which was about the equivalent of seven o'clock in Vienna and the minister a couple of hours later.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: You might point out I was in Vancouver.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The Minister of Fisheries was in Vancouver and that was why I felt I ought to get in touch with my wife because I could get in touch with her at a much earlier hour than I could get through to the Minister of Fisheries on account of the three-hour difference in time. It is quite complicated when you are telephoning between Vienna and Vancouver. By the most extraordinary coincidence-it is a coincidence if you are using the trans-Atlantic telephone service-my wife did call me at seven o'clock on Sunday evening. I suggested to her that she get in touch with the Minister of Fisheries in Vancouver and ask him if he could not make arrangements to have this faculty moved to British Columbia and affiliated with the university and make provision for shelter for them there and let me know before midnight. And he did that. I do not think that sort of thing has been done very often.
I may say that on Sunday evening last these professors and students passed through Ottawa. I believe they are now in Abbotsford and that their next stage is to go to Powell River where they are to set up housekeeping for a while and learn English.
When I had felt that I had done everything I reasonably could in Vienna I left by motor car about eight o'clock in the evening and drove about 200 miles into western Austria. I slept in a small hotel and next morning went on to the place where these students were. I put to them the offer that my colleague had passed to me the day before and after a good deal of discussion back and forth during which I tried to explain the virtues of British Columbia-

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Easy.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
-and some of the advantages there would be for them and for us I went away with their acceptance of the offer. I also discovered when I got to this place near Salzburg where they were staying that there were in addition somewhere between 100 and 150 other university students, students of mining engineering, oil engineering, geology and various other sciences, and several professors, who also expressed interest
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in coming to Canada. They expressed a desire to be together in Canada and I told them I would endeavour to find some place where they could go and be together. I could make no promise but I told them I would see what I could do. I said that I did not think it would be reasonable to suggest that they should also go to British Columbia and that I thought it would be to some other place.
As soon as I could do so, I got in touch with my colleague, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence, (Mr. Hellyer) and arranged with him to have one of these students go to Toronto. I may say that my hon. friend put him up in his own house and looked after him for about two weeks so that he might look around and see what might be possible. The hon. gentleman got in touch with the president of the University of Toronto. He also got in touch with a number of prominent businessmen in Toronto, and a very generous offer was made for the reception of these professors and students.
Meanwhile I had also communicated with the chancellor of my own university, the University of Manitoba, about these students at a time when I was not quite sure where they might go. When I arrived in Paris a few days later I had a telephone call from Mr. Sifton and the premier of Manitoba, who were together. They had thought that this group represented a complete faculty and they made a most generous offer, for which I personally shall always be grateful, and of which I shall always be proud, to bring this group of students and professors to Manitoba and look after them completely for a certain period.
In the meantime news reports about this group of students had got out in Canada and we also had offers from Ottawa University, Laval University and several other places where there were not actually universities but where people hoped that this group of students might be the nucleus for something. All these offers did pose a bit of a problem. The young student who had come here as the spokesman of the students visited the various universities. I felt the only way to do was to have him visit the universities, compare the offers and communicate with the other students, and the decision they finally made was to go to Toronto. I may say that this group of students has either arrived in Toronto or will arrive there before the end of the day.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
They arrived this
morning.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I should like to add, though I am breaking my narrative by saying this,
664	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that there are also a good number of other students in Vienna, and elsewhere in Austria, who are seeking to come to Canada or the United States in order to complete their studies, and there are at the present time about 100 oi them in Montreal. The national conference of Canadian universities has set up a committee to review the qualifications of these students and to examine all the offers of assistance which have been received, in the hope, as far as possible, of finding offers of assistance that will fit with the qualifications of the persons concerned, with a view to having them placed in various universities throughout the country. I do not know whether the number of offers received is as yet equal to the number of students who are in Canada. That is one reason why I felt I would like to say something here about the situation, in the hope that my words might go beyond this chamber and perhaps might not, in all cases, fall on entirely deaf ears. It does seem to me that in the light of all the concern that was being expressed in this country only a few short months ago as a result of that very interesting conference at St. Andrews, it would be a very unfortunate thing if we in Canada missed the opportunity of getting young people who are almost completely trained-people who have only to learn one of the official languages of this country and who, because most of them are quite bright, could probably do that in a few months by modern intensive methods. It would, as I say, be a pity if we did not allow ourselves to take advantage of this opportunity to enrich our country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I will return to my narrative and shall try to make it brief.
I had announced, of course, at the very beginning of this movement of Hungarian refugees, that all our offices in Europe would give priority to applications from these people. After I had seen what I did see in Vienna-the fact that at the time I was there there were 70,000 of these refugees still in Austria, and that the numbers entering every day were at least equal to the numbers taken away-it seemed to me that we should not take refugees, except sponsored cases, from any of the countries of secondary refuge while the problem in Austria was so acute. I felt it would be desirable to see what the situation was in the offices in the neighbouring countries, and I wanted, moreover- though this is not strictly relevant to the present discussion-to see what the prospects were in these countries for immigration this year.
I found in Germany that the German government had set no limit on the number of refugees they were willing to take, but


they were having difficulty in finding accommodation for them. However, they did want to keep them all because they have an acute shortage of labour. In these circumstances I gave instructions that no visas were to be issued except to those refugees who had Canadian sponsors who were prepared to look after them.
In Holland, where I went next, I found that the government of The Netherlands had agreed to take 3,000 and keep them in the country, and they did not want these people disturbed. But they did feel that they had room to give temporary refuge to 2,000 more, and they had apparently made some representations to Ottawa, as well as to Washington and Canberra about this situation. I had thought of the same idea as appeared to be in their minds while I was at Bonn the night before, and when I proposed this plan to the Dutch minister he said: "We have already suggested that to your government." We had some discussion during the afternoon and then he came to dine at the embassy. I was able to get my colleague, the Minister of Finance on the telephone, and we agreed it would be quite within the terms of reference under which I was acting if I undertook to move to Canada between the 1st of March and midsummer at least 3,000 from Holland. The Dutch came to the conclusion that they could only find shelter for 2,000, and we made an arrangement under which that number of people are being moved to Holland now. The first 500 have already arrived in Holland. These 2,000 will begin coming to Canada in Dutch ships in small numbers after the 1st of March and until the end of June.
This arrangement seems to me to have the great advantage of getting 2,000 more people out of Austria reasonably quickly and also of keeping them in Europe during the winter when, as I do not need to remind any hon. member, it is very difficult for us to accommodate large numbers of new people in Canada.
I next went to Belgium, where I found that the situation was somewhat similar to the situation in Germany. They were not able to take an unlimited number of refugees, but they wanted to keep those they had. They had employment for them. The decision we took in this case, therefore, was that from then on we would accept only sponsored cases.
When I got to Paris I found that the situation in France was really very difficult. I think that, perhaps, hon. members may be interested to know why. The French, with the characteristic generosity in humanitarian matters which that country has always shown, had agreed to accept Hungarian refugees

without any limit as to numbers, and . about
8,000	or 9,000 of them had already arrived in France. The only places in which they could be lodged quickly were military barracks, and any hon. member who has had experience of French barracks knows there are more hospitable places in the world than the average caserne. Some of these barracks were also occupied by French troops; there were sentries on duty, and some of the refugees got the impression that they had left one prison in Budapest to go to another prison in France. This impression was intensified by the most unfortunate kind of communist propaganda, so much so that when I met the minister of the interior, under whose department these people are being cared for, he asked me to get Canadians to visit these camps to tell the people there that France was not a communist country; that it was not a "people's democracy" but a real democracy. The French wanted these people to stay, and wanted them to work, but would have no objection to their going away to any other country if that country would take them. He asked me to accept some immediately as a token of the truth of this.
Well, under the policy of priority I have enunciated earlier we had agreed to take a certain number of them, and I naturally did not countermand anything that had been done; but I explained that I did not really think it would be proper to take refugees from France, a country which was able to look after them, while leaving such a great burden on Austria. I felt the best we could do would be to send our officials round as quickly as possible, and indicate that we would come later with teams and give people visas that would be valid after April 1. By that time, it seemed to me, we would be able to absorb them in Canada: by that time, also, we hoped there would be a clarification of the situation in Austria. In any event the problem in Austria itself would not be so great during the summer months. This was very acceptable to the French government, and we agreed to take up to 3,000 providing the French would take a corresponding number from Austria in the interval, and that policy is now being worked out.
When I reached England I found that the situation was not quite as bad as in France, but it was very nearly so. Britain had had to suspend the actual movement of refugees because there were no places readily available for accommodation. The British government and people had made a magnificent effort; they had moved 12,000 people to the United Kingdom, 6,000 of them in about three days by a really drastic airlift which was going on while I was actually in Vienna. But they were finding a lot of difficulty of one kind or
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration another in that many of these people claimed they had been promised they could go to the United States or Canada. They were very disappointed when they found they were still in Europe. I recall particularly hearing of one group who were taken to Scotland-I am sure the hon. member for Greenwood would be interested in this-and when they asked where they were they were shown Scotland on the map. They said Oh, this is too close to Russia; we want to get across the Atlantic at once.
In any event, our high commissioner had been approached by the British government to ascertain if we would start taking some of these people to Canada right away. We arranged a meeting with the people who were actually looking after the refugees-they were voluntary agencies exclusively-and with the home office which had official charge of them. While I was not able to conclude an agreement while I was there I did make an offer which was accepted a day or two after I returned to Canada. Our offer was to take 5,000 from the United Kingdom after April 1 on the understanding that the British would, as quickly as possible, resume taking refugees from Austria and would take a corresponding number. This understanding was arrived at in good faith and I am sure will be carried out by both sides.
While I was abroad I had arranged for the transportation to Canada, between the time I was there and the end of January, of 9,000 to 10,000 Hungarian refugees. I felt that it would not be prudent or sensible for me to go beyond that until I returned to Ottawa and found out the response that was being made and how things were being organized or until I had an opportunity to consult with my colleagues and determined what they felt would be a reasonable flow to maintain during the winter months. As soon as possible after my return to Ottawa I consulted my colleagues and I recommended that we should make immediate arrangements for another
2,000	to come by sea in February and for the maintenance of the Maritime Central flights. This was the only Canadian company that was willing to continue these flights beyond January 1 because both T.C.A. and C.P.A. had other commitments for which their aircraft would be required. It was understood also that, as soon as we had some experience as to how these people were going to be placed and how we could distribute them throughout the country, we would consider taking more.
It began to appear to me early in January, while I was still recovering from the effect of having had a chip taken off my shoulder in the hospital, that we could quite easily

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration take another 1,000 people by sea in late January and February, so another thousand was added to the number. More recently my colleagues authorized me to go ahead and make arrangements for another 2,000 to come to Canada in March. I should say that in addition to these numbers there are always a certain number of sponsored cases that are being handled in small numbers by ordinary airlines and by ordinary sea passages which, week after week, do mount up to something. Our best estimate at the moment is that we will have more than 15,000 Hungarian refugees in Canada by the end of February, and that we will have between 2,000 and 3,000 more coming in March. Then, we will still have these 10,000 that are being staged in the three countries I have mentioned.
This does not mean at all that we are going to stop taking people from Austria after March. Our position is, as it has been throughout in this matter, that we intend to take these people as long as they want to come here and it looks as though we can find accommodation for them and, in a reasonable time, find work for them. We are going to take them as rapidly as we think they can be reasonably readily absorbed. I think it would be imprudent to try to make hard and fast arrangements too far in advance. We do intend to follow that course.
I should like to indicate very briefly, if I am not taking up too much of the time of the committee, sir, what the proportion of those coming to Canada is compared with the overall situation so far as Hungarian refugees are concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I might take the opportunity provided at this moment to advise the minister that his time has expired.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Has the minister leave to continue?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I will say a word and then the minister can continue.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Kamloops. I shall try not to exceed my time again, sir. There have been approximately 170,000-I should like hon. members just to consider that figure for a moment-[DOT] about half of the population of metropolitan Ottawa, of these Hungarian refugees enter Austria since November 4. They have entered a country of between six million and seven million people, a poor country and a country that had very little surplus accommodation. About 100,000 of these refugees have left Austria for other countries. The largest single group has gone to the United States. There have been, as I think hon. members


probably know, 6,500 admitted to the United States as immigrants and 15,000 admitted as parolees. Do not ask me to explain what a parolee is because I am not an expert on United States immigration matters. I sincerely hope, and I am inclined to believe, that the United States is going to take more. But up to now, that is what they have done, and that is not as large a number as we are definitely committed to take. We are committed to take over 25,000 already.
I should think that next after the United States would be the British, and they have taken about 12,000. This will be about the total number they will take unless there is some big change in policy, because what they are taking from now on is merely a matter of substitution. The French and the Germans have still put no upper limit on the number they will take. About 10,000 have gone to France and about 10,000 to Germany. Other countries have taken a considerably smaller number. At the moment the only country that is taking any considerable number of people out of Austria is Canada, either by direct movement to Canada or indirectly. Measured in terms of numbers, therefore, we have committed ourselves already to take between 1/6 and 1/7 of those who have come into Austria.
In terms of the monetary commitments that we have made so far in connection with this matter, assuming that the house agrees to this estimate, we will have spent proportionately very much more than any other country, including the United States; not absolutely, but proportionately more. I believe it is necessary to say these things, not because I want to suggest we have done too much or that we have done all we could or should do, but I would suggest that if we are going to view this problem in anything like its proper proportions it is only fair to the Canadian taxpayers who are paying for this movement that they should know what they are getting and what they are paying.
I should now like to say a word or two about something which is really a good deal more relevant to the estimate here, and that is the problem of settlement. We have had the most magnificent co-operation from voluntary organizations all over this country and I cannot speak too highly of them. There have been times when I think all of us have felt, everybody connected with the movement, that there could be and should be a little more co-ordination, but I have taken the view that it is not the proper function of the immigration department to try to organize that co-ordination on a national basis. The problems of settlement are local

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
problems all over the country and much better results will be obtained through proper local initiatives. We have tried to co-operate with everybody who is willing to help. We have tried to make every suggestion we could about the most effective way of organizing that co-operation but we have not tried to run the show. We have tried to fit our activities into the voluntary activities. I think that is the right way to do it.
One or two misconceptions have arisen as a result of an agreement we made with the government of Saskatchewan, which was made by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, who was acting for me while I was abroad and for which we are very grateful to the government of Saskatchewan. It was a businesslike arrangement made in a businesslike way. Under that arrangement we did agree to pay to the government of Saskatchewan $3 a day for each of the refugees while they were in the provincial reception centres. Because of this, and because we have agreed to do something similar in other provinces where reception centres are set up, if they are needed, I am told that a misconception has arisen in certain parts of this country which I should like to clear up now, namely, that every Hungarian gets $3 a day as soon as he comes to the country. I am told there are places where that is widely believed.
Well, it is not true at all; they are not getting anything. The money is paid to the provincial government, or to whoever is operating the reception centre, for the services rendered in that centre. And where we provide subsistence, as we do for Hungarians, like other immigrants who cannot support themselves in the first year in the country, we do not pay money to the immigrant receiving the subsistence, we pay the bills and we do not pay $3 a day. We get it done just as cheaply as we can get it done respectably, and will continue to do so. In fact, nothing is being done for the Hungarian refugees that is not done for other immigrants once they land in Canada. It is true that they get their way paid to the place where they come to settle. That is the only respect in which they are given treatment different from that of any other immigrants.
Another misconception that has arisen, and it was given a good deal of unnecessary currency, I think, by one or two people whose activities seemed to me to be almost mischievous-was that we were giving to those refugees free health care which was being denied to Canadians.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: That is true.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Well, it is not true at all.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: For one year.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
No, it is not true for one year. The hon. member for Cape Breton South is not aware of the real facts. Hungarians and other immigrants are treated in the same way as Canadians are; if they are indigents they do not go without treatment. But if they have an income they pay their bills like anybody else, and that is the situation. We do not go around looking for bills to pay, either.
I do not think it would be the sense of this house, or the sense of the country, that we should treat immigrants better than we treat our own people. I do not think it would be the sense of the house or the sense of the country that they should be treated worse. These are people who have come

and I am not referring here specifically to Hungarian refugees but to immigrants generally-to this country and whom we have accepted, and given a landing to, on the assumption that they are going eventually to become fellow citizens of ours. I think the sooner we treat them on a basis of equality the better.
The reason the federal government does certain of these things in the first year is that, for many kinds of welfare services in this country, a year is the ordinary period required to acquire domicile within local jurisdictions. That is the reason it is done and the only reason. I felt it would be useful to say these things in the hope that the facts may catch up with some of the rumours.
We are asking in this item for $9 million. It would be optimistic to think that this $9 million was going to cover the whole cost of this operation. We had certain money. I notice the hon. member for Perth, who was here a moment or two ago, is not in the chamber just at this moment. During the discussion of the regular estimates I think he accused me of padding one of the items and I said at that time I hoped that the amount would never be used because it was there for an emergency. Well, sir, unfortunately, unhappily, tragically, the emergency happened and we were very glad to have that money because it has tided us over pretty nearly until now.
We are asking for another $9 million now and we are spending out of our regular votes and using our regular services for these refugees, and I do not think we can begin to estimate all the costs there will be in this movement before the autumn. But it will be considerably more than $9 million and I think it is only fair to tell the committee that right now.
I do think-and I imagine that every hon. member who has seen at least some of these

668	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Hungarian refugees also thinks-that we are going to get full value for our money. I want to say this. I think there will be some people among these Hungarian refugees who will be undesirable; I think there will be some bad eggs among them; I think that is inevitable and I think it is better to face that fact right now. I do hope, too, that the few cases

because I believe there will be few- that are disappointing will not be unduly magnified, at any rate, by responsible people. I am sure they will not be by any member of the house. The great majority of these people are-if I can judge people at allbright and vigorous. They are intelligent and a good proportion of them have some skill. The great handicap they have is that very few can speak either English or French. When they have got over that handicap I believe they will be as good immigrants as any, as good settlers and ultimately as good citizens as any we have ever had and I think in the long run they will enrich this country.
There is just one other thing, sir. While again this is not quite strictly relevant, yet I think I ought to say a word about it. There has been a good deal in the newspapers lately about the transportation problem that is likely to arise in the late spring. We anticipated this problem in the immigration department away back last August, long before this Hungarian problem added to it, and we have been in touch with steamship companies and the air lines with respect to it ever since. I had a conference with a number of steamship companies when I was in London and we have had a number of other conversations, and we are going to have to take special and extraordinary measures to move the regular flow of immigration which is going to be larger than usual this year, apart from the Hungarians. But I believe we are going to find the means to do it and certainly we are going to make every conceivable effort to find the means to do it because, as my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated more than once, we have a bigger program of capital expansion this year than ever before, and one of the biggest shortages that we will experience later this year is almost certainly going to be a shortage of manpower and we want to get all we can in order to maintain the expansion we have had in the last few years.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure there will be no one in the house who will not agree with the purpose for which the $9 million is being requested in the supplementary estimate, though there may be and I think there properly are some criticisms and quite serious suggestions that could be made

as to the method by which the matter has been handled to date and how it should be handled in the future.
If I voice some of those criticisms I want to say at the outset that I hope it is not going to be taken as indicating any disagreement with the purpose for which the money is sought and for which the sum the minister referred to has already been spent, because I am quite sure all hon. members of the house as well as the country generally agree that not only will these people coming from Hungary enrich our country, as has been the case with all the other immigrants we have received, but it is Canada's duty as a nation of the world to make some contribution to the solution of this problem.
We have some criticisms to offer, though, and they are serious criticisms; and if I say that in listening to the minister today, in listening to him on previous occasions, and in reading reports of his trip to Vienna one of the criticisms that has occurred to us is that perhaps there has been a little too much use of the first person singular and a little too much suggestion of personal credit for what is being done, that is perhaps a minor matter and not one of the serious criticisms we have in mind.
I think probably the best place to start is the point where the minister concluded, and that is with respect to the settlement arrangements here in Canada. I am sure that all on this side of the house feel that, except in so far as the difficulties of the situation make it necessary, these immigrants should not be dealt with in any way different from normal immigrants, and should not be given any special privileges over and above Canadians. I deliberately used the qualification "except in so far as the special circumstances of this movement make it necessary" because this surely cannot be regarded as an ordinary movement of immigrants.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Oh, quite.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The minister has pointed out that in this movement, if in fact it is not to be properly described as a crash operation,
170,000	persons have already fled from Hungary into Austria, a country very much smaller, very much poorer and very much more crowded than Canada and many other countries in the western civilization, and that we cannot leave Austria to grapple with that situation too long because it must be dealt with as an operation calling for immediate action. I also want to say that I accept the fact that there were bound to be mistakes, shortcomings and deficiencies in the handling

of the problem to date, and it would not be fair or responsible not to accept that fact and to criticize the government because they tried to do something even before they had satisfactorily worked out all the details. As a matter of fact my criticism rather goes the other way in that-

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: We have been too timid.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
No, but having been willing to accept the risks and to face the fact that it is going to create problems, the government is not doing enough now to solve the problems which have been created. I think it was inescapable that there would be problems, particularly concerning the reception and settlement in Canada of these people, but I am not at all satisfied that enough is now being done to meet those problems. I do not accept the minister's statement that it is not the proper function of the immigration department to try to co-ordinate the problem on a national basis.
In the ordinary course of immigration, which under the policy of the government certainly cannot be said to be overly vigorous, the reception and settlement arrangements for immigrants can probably best be made on a local basis. Where you have an emergency movement such as this I do not think it is at all sensible to suggest that the reception and settlement arrangements should best be left to be handled on a local basis, and that there is no responsibility on the part of the department to co-ordinate them on a national basis. That is exactly thf responsibility that exists in a situation such as this.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair, and perhaps we could save a lot of time by not quarrelling about terms. As far as settlement is concerned, that responsibility is accepted by my department. I was talking about reception and welfare and things that are done incidental to the arrival and between the time of arrival and settlement.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I will go on from there to say that here again I think we must face the fact that these immigrants are probably not going to be able to fit into the stream of Canadian employment, activity and life as quickly as the great majority of normal immigrants who come to Canada. We must remember that to a large extent these people are not coming to Canada in the full sense of the words "of their own free will". They are coming as the result of a tragedy which occurred in Hungary, to use the minister's words, and many of them are coming entirely unprepared, never having thought before of the possibility of emigrating. In
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration many cases they are coming without having at their disposal the means which many normal immigrants have, and so it cannot be expected that they will be fitted into the ordinary pattern of Canadian life as quickly as the majority of normal immigrants.
For that reason it seems to me we have to accept a greater responsibility for looking after these people than is normally the case, and that is necessary not only in fairness to them but I believe it is essential in protecting the legitimate interests of Canadians who are already here. I do not think it is fair to the Hungarian refugee to turn him out too quickly into the normal stream of Canadian employment, nor would it be fair to those employers who are supposed to accept him or his fellow workers, the employees who are interested in working alongside him and interested also in the job he will be filling. While we accept that there will be shortcomings in the initial phases of this movement, as I have said, my criticism is that I do not see sufficient signs of action being taken at this time to deal with the problem and remove those shortcomings.
I have not seen a great many of these immigrants myself but I have seen some of them, and I have spoken to others who have seen many more. One of the things which I do not think is being attended to nearly rapidly enough is the problem of education in our languages. Those whom I say arrived in Canada with an immigration sheet, a list of phrases and words in Hungarian and English; one sheet, that was all. Up to the time I left them we had not been able to find out what plans were made to provide them with a more adequate phrase sheet, or to organize classes for them where they might learn the language.
I do not suppose that there exists a great quantity of Hungarian-English dictionaries in Canada. It seems to me that sort of thing is one of the responsibilities which this department should meet; that is, the provision to the local welfare organizations of an adequate supply of material, whether it be mimeographed sheets or printed books, which would enable the instruction of Hungarians in the English and French languages. There should be more than normal attention paid to the organization of classes for these people.
Remember that the ordinary stream of immigration to Canada in the last few years has averaged, I think, somewhere just under 150,000. Now we are committed to take an additional 28,000, and it is quite possible that we will take at least 30,000 or 40,000 in one year; that is one-fifth more than our normal intake, all in one group. It is going to take more than the normal effort to instruct these

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration people in the Canadian approach, Canadian skills and Canadian way of life, let alone the English or French languages. I do not think that responsibility can be left to the local citizens' welfare organizations, Canadian citizenship societies and the other organizations which normally make themselves responsible to a considerable extent for that work.
Here it is obvious, I believe, that the department must accept a greater responsibility itself and make greater efforts to assist these people; otherwise these refugees will not be able to fit into the Canadian pattern as they should. Here we have what you might call quite properly a crash operation in which the department are going to have to accept a great deal more responsibility and expend a great deal more effort than they have done up to the present.
That raises the question of camps or reception facilities. Here we are in the winter months accepting a very large addition to the normal flow of immigrants, at a time when employment opportunities in Canada are normally much more restricted than in the summer months. I do not think it is sufficient to say we will leave it to the generosity of private individuals to receive and care for these people until such time as employment opportunities increase in the summer. That may be a period of up to six months or more.
I think the department must make an assessment of the situation and endeavour to find accommodation, even if it be in the nature of temporary camps, and I do not mean a tent camp or anything of that sort. There are areas in Canada where such buildings exist and where the instruction of these refugees would be facilitated a great deal more than if they were scattered about in individual homes, where this type of work is so much more difficult to co-ordinate.
I think there also must be more attention given to informing these men and women when they arrive just what plans are made and what facilities are available for their instruction and their placement, because those whom I have seen and spoken to were warmly received by the Canadians into whose homes they went; they were marvellous people to have. As the minister stated, most of them had skills. All they wanted was not to be a burden on the people in whose homes they found lodging. Their greatest concern was that they did not want to take charity; they wanted to be able to earn their way in Canada as soon as possible. They were almost desperate about finding out what arrangements had been made for their instruction. The people with whom they were living tried to assure them that they would be welcome 

there as long as they wanted to stay, but the more Canadians tried to show them that they need not worry for the time being, that they would be glad to have them stay, the more the Hungarians felt that Canadians were trying to show them charity. They appreciated the charity, but they did not want to come to this country and be accused of expecting nothing but charity.
Something must be done to make available much more rapidly than is the case now facilities for instructing these people and fitting them into our pattern of Canadian life. I do not mean to fit them in more rapidly, but rather to start more rapidly to instruct them as to how to go about fitting in.
Another reason I am convinced that the provision of accommodation is a responsibility which we must accept is because of the growing problem in Austria. Unless we are able to receive them they will pile up in the camps in Austria. I have not been there; the minister has. Mr. Michael Barkway, one of the members of the press gallery, has also been there; he and the minister do not seem to agree in their opinion as to conditions in Austria and Canadian responsibility in the matter.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I do not think there is any disagreement between us as to the conditions in Austria.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I am glad to hear that. Then I take it that the disagreement is in what we must do about relieving conditions more rapidly than is being done now. Certainly Mr. Barkway suggests that unless something is done to keep the stream moving quickly, not only will Hungarian refugees themselves suffer from sad disillusionment, which would be a bad start, but the whole cause of freedom will suffer because the communist propagandists in that area will then be able to say that all this talk about the western nations receiving these people is only talk. If the refugees were left to languish in Austria there would then be a condition in Austria which would be disastrous. Therefore I do not think it is enough for us just to say that we are taking more than the United States in proportion. We have proportionately more room than the United States.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I do not agree with that.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I do not think we should take pride in that fact and leave it at that. We have to assess our own capabilities to deal with the matter and then fulfil the obligation which that assessment imposes upon us.
While we are happy that the $9 million is being asked for, I do not think it is going to be wisely spent unless some greater

responsibility is accepted by the federal department of immigration with respect to the reception, settlement and accommodation arrangements here, and particularly the instruction arrangements here. I believe that now is the time to plan those arrangements, so we may not only continue but in fact speed up the movement to Canada of those refugees we are prepared to take. I think our efforts should be directed to getting over here as quickly as possible the number that we decide should be accepted in Canada. Another question which occurs to me-it is a matter of detail, but I would like the minister to deal with it-is whether we are accepting refugees in Austria solely through our immigration office or whether we are going out into the camps-

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I did answer that the other day in reply to a question.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I think the minister must expand on the subject. I know he referred to it. This is one of the points that concerned Mr. Barkway at the time of his visit. What drive is being made to go right into the camps and set up the necessary facilities there, and show these people that we mean what we say when we offer to provide a home for them in Canada? That would seem to me to call for an increase in staff, because it would mean manning two offices instead of one. Can the minister not tell us the details of the work being done there?
The other question I have is one of a general nature. What is the total number of refugees who are expected to move into Austria, and is it expected that the movement will continue at the same pace as in the past? At one time I understand that the refugee figure amounted to about 1,000 a day. Has anyone attempted, or is it felt that anyone could attempt, to estimate the total number of refugees who may be involved? What is the estimate of the number Canada feels she can take and that will be available to us?
Those, I think, are questions which should be answered now in order that the problems of settlement may be discussed in the light of that information. Whatever the problem may be, as I have said-and I think this is the point that requires to be emphasized- this cannot be regarded as a normal movement, and the responsibilities of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration for coordinating the reception and settlement of these people are far greater than the minister seems to indicate he is prepared to accept.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS

Had you not interceded in defence of the rules, Mr. Chairman, I was going to suggest that if I were to be guided by precedent already established during this debate, I would find it utterly impossible to determine the bounds within which I must keep in the course of my observations. I know, Mr. Chairman, that traditionally it is the duty of the opposition to criticize. This is a privilege I would not take away from the opposition, nor would I do anything to discourage them even on this occasion. Moreover, I may say that if there is one minister in the House of Commons who can provoke criticism it is the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
However, upon this occasion I find it extremely difficult to be very critical. I say that, Mr. Chairman, because of the fact that we are dealing with those who are the victims of probably one of the most tragic situations ever to occur in this world. We are dealing with babies, little children, mothers and others who have done two things. First, they have given this world one of the finest demonstrations it has ever witnessed of just how much people who have lost their freedom value it. Furthermore, this occurrence has been an indication to those of us who are free just what is our responsibility in retaining it. Second, we are dealing with people who have done more than all others to unmask communism and indicate to the world the true nature of that vicious force.
I agree with some of the things said by the hon. member for Kamloops, but after all we are dealing with an emergency; something which has happened suddenly; something that must be dealt with immediately. If some of these things were to occur in the course of our ordinary immigration policy, the handling of immigrants who come here under normal circumstances, then I too would be rather severely critical. I am not going to be critical here. I do not expect us to be able to handle these people in exactly the same way as we would handle normal immigrants.
The minister mentioned that, proportionately, Canada had already accepted more of 82715-43J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration these Hungarian refugees than had the United States; that is undoubtedly true. I believe Canada is probably in a position to handle more of them than the United States will ever handle. I say that not from the standpoint of our ability or inability to finance them but because of the very nature of our country, economically and geographically, and the fact that we have been led to believe it is so extremely important for Canada to build up her population as rapidly as it is reasonably possible to do so.
Plainly I cannot subscribe to some of the observations of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I rather fancied that perhaps I misunderstood them; I hope I did not, but I cannot be certain until I examine the record and determine exactly what he said. Actually, Mr. Chairman, I rose in order to ask the minister a question or two. I am merely seeking information. I wonder if his department is yet in a position to indicate the disposition of these Hungarian immigrants across Canada by provinces. I think we should have that information. Secondly, I should like to have information with respect to the age groups, the sexes, the professions, occupations and so on. I would appreciate having that. I feel that probably the house would benefit as a consequence of receiving it. I am sure if the minister has the information he would be pleased to put it on the record.
I am not going to take up more time. Last November we as a group endorsed what the government indicated to us it was prepared to do. We feel that, to be fair, they have done a pretty good job of it. We realize that there are a lot of difficulties to be ironed out. We feel, as I said, that the government has done a pretty good job of it; but we also feel that the provinces, cities, towns, municipalities, voluntary organizations and individuals also have done a pretty good job and are continuing to do so. We hope any bugs that are appearing will be removed, and we expect they will. Probably in a month or two we shall be in a better position to assess the whole situation, and if with respect to certain things we do appear to be mildly critical we can assure the minister it will only be because we would be justified in being so. It is too early in the game for hon. members to be advancing some of the criticisms to which we have already listened.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the hon. member who has just taken his seat on having some Christian common sense. I congratulate the government on the job they have done. They were certainly not slow or lazy; they jumped into the job
676	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration right at once, and I congratulate the government on sending the young minister over there to find out for himself, as he did. One thing I am surprised at is that the expert critic of the opposition has not been able to find more mistakes because of the vastness of the undertaking. But since Canada is a Christian country it is her duty to feed the hungry, clothe the naked and help those who are out of joint with the rest of the world.
I congratulate these refugees on the stand they have taken against Russia. It will live forever in the history of Hungary. We have a Hungarian committee in Fort William, as I mentioned before. We had the opportunity of taking a group of these refugees. Donald Clark and Son, of Port Arthur, who had bought the Great Lakes sawmill, had a number of houses that were formerly used to house Japanese who came from Vancouver and used the houses to shelter these people. The reception they received was certainly pleasing to the Hungarians. They were met by the mayors of both cities and by others, and they were well received and well fed. The clergy, both Protestant and Roman Catholic, representing this group, called on them. I know the majority of them are Roman Catholic, but that does not make any difference; they can be hungry, and they can be out of work.
Another thing is that many people thought there would be many communists among them. Anybody who has come out of Hungary under these circumstances is cured forever of being a communist. I congratulate the government and the young minister on the job they are doing, and hope they will keep on doing it.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think all hon. members were very interested in the minister's remarks. I found one thing he said very interesting, namely the reference he made to the group of students coming to Toronto today. I think he made reference to the fact that they had not yet landed but were going to do so. I am sorry the minister did not elaborate a little further on that particular subject, because many of us would like to know the number of students who are coming to Toronto; whether the government is going to pay for them or some private concern will pay for them; where they are going to stay while they are attending the university, and so on. I think we should like to hear about it from the human interest point of view.
The minister said these students are coming. I think some hon. members have heard stories about this arrangement. I have had some information which suggested that there


would be about 109 students arriving, and that a great deal of the expense of their education was going to be paid by the Ontario mining association. I would be very glad if the minister could confirm or deny it.
When the minister was dealing with this matter of the students he made reference to the hon. member for Davenport and the fine liaison work he had done to help them along. I think the minister may have been a little less than generous in not giving some credit to the Ontario government, particularly to the department of planning and development. It is my understanding that they also had quite a lot to do with this particular arrangement.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Not this particular one; in the reception of the Hungarians generally, yes, but not this particular one. It was the president of the university and a group of businessmen who were approached directly by the hon. member about this matter. With respect to the refugees generally, I give full credit to the Ontario government for what they have done.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: That answers my question. The Ontario government actually had nothing to do with the mining students from Sopron University?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Not in the early stages; I believe they have been very helpful lately.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
There is one thing I would like to bring to the minister's attention now rather than do it privately, as ordinarily I probably would have done. I think it is something that should be brought to his attention and to the attention of the country generally because, while it is only one situation, I have no doubt it could be duplicated in a number of places. The situation I am going to refer to has arisen because of a misunderstanding which, if it were cleared up now, would probably save a lot of grief for a number of people in this country in the future.
I refer to a letter I received the other day from a constituent of mine. His name is Mr. John Gyurki. He lives in Woodstock, and is a Canadian citizen of Hungarian extraction. I quote two paragraphs from the letter which I think are important. They read as follows:
On December 14 last, I brought six members of my family to Canada from Hungary. To acquire sufficient funds to pay for their passage, I had to borrow money from the bank. I understood that the passage for refugees would be paid by the government, as pointed out in numerous newspaper clippings, some dated November 29 last. Two of these clippings are enclosed to you herewith.

I might say at this point that I shall refer to these clippings later. I continue with the letter:
In these clippings, the Honourable John W. Pickersgill stated that a decision had been made to grant free passage not only to those refugees yet to come, but to those already arrived or on route.
The next paragraph reads:
After inquiring about free transportation to Canada with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, I received a letter from them dated January 10 last, which I am enclosing. I cannot see any comparison between the contents of that letter and the newspaper clippings:	they just
don't correspond. I refer especially to the second paragraph of the letter.
I refer to the second paragraph of the letter which was sent to Mr. Gyurki, dated January 10 last, by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and it reads in part as follows:
I have your letter of January 4, 1957, enclosing six air contract tickets covering the transportation to Canada of five members of your family at a total cost of $1,035.
Free transportation to Canada in respect of Hungarian refugees does not apply where persons pay their own transportation to Canada or where the cost of their transportation is advanced by a friend or a relative in this country.
The remainder of the letter is not particularly relevant to this discussion. As a member of this house, Mr. Chairman, I understood that these were the regulations at the time, and I have no doubt that other hon. members had that understanding. But unfortunately the general public does not have the advantage of the sources of information that hon. members have, and very often- in fact most of the time-the public rely on what they read in the newspapers. I would like to refer to a couple of clippings which are enclosed in the letter. One is from the Toronto Star, dated November 29. It also contains a large picture of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and reads as follows:
Ottawa, November 29-Canada will not only open its gates to all Hungarian refugees who want to come here, but will provide their passage free, Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, told the House of Commons last night.
His announcement was greeted by cheers from all sections of the house, and welcomed by opposition speakers.
Until yesterday afternoon, the government had planned only to give the refugees "assisted passage", which was expected to be repaid.
Decision to give passage as a gift was made at a cabinet meeting yesterday afternoon, Mr. Pickersgill said. The decision applies not only to those yet to come, but to those who have already arrived or are en route.
I have another press clipping to which I shall refer very briefly. It is a Canadian Press dispatch which appeared under the same date line in the Woodstock daily Sentinel-Review. The quotation reads:
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration "It was decided," Mr. Pickersgill said, "that as almost all of these refugees have nothing they can bring with them except the clothes they are wearing, and, as many of them have little or no money, it was not reasonable to expect them to try to establish themselves in this country with a debt over their heads at the very start."
This policy of free passage would also apply to Hungarian refugees who have already had assisted passage to Canada-a small number as yet.
This is a very unfortunate situation, and there are probably a number of other people in the same situation as Mr. Gyurki of Woodstock. I was going to say there were others who had been victimized, but that word possibly has an unpleasant connotation. Doubtless there are others who have been misled by these press reports. Probably they should have made inquiries of the minister, but perhaps it was not possible to reach him because he might not have been available at the time. It is most unfortunate that these people should have borrowed money to bring to this country what in this case were not even close relatives, and relied on the press reports. As a result of having brought these Hungarians to Canada they are now in debt to the bank.
I am raising this point today in the hope that other people will not fall into the same trap, and I think the minister might consider as special cases those who went into debt in this way. Perhaps reimbursement could be made to these people who borrowed money in good faith in order to bring relatives and friends to Canada in an honest and sincere desire to be of help. I am not suggesting that the minister created this impression deliberately, but an unfortunate impression was created in the press and I hope the minister will be sympathetic toward this case and any others that might turn up.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the minister if he would allow me to do so. My question concerns the Hungarian immigrants who have been accepted in Canada up to the present time. Can the minister tell me how many were under nine years of age? Before the minister rises to answer my question I wish to say a few words about a group of young Hungarian immigrants who were admitted into this country.
Under the auspices of the bishop of Nicolet, His Excellency Monsignor Martin, a group of people were organized to receive young Hungarian immigrants, and already 600 have been taken in by families some of whom had five or six children or more. I might also point out that the demand for these unhappy young immigrants has been greater than the number who are available. The group has encountered one problem and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration it is the following. It is the desire of those families who have taken children into their homes to adopt the refugees, but according to the law of the province of Quebec the adoption cannot be legalized if the parents of the children are alive.
I would be grateful to the minister if an inquiry could be conducted as quickly as possible to learn whether the parents of these children are living or dead. If they are dead it will be very easy to have the refugee children legally adopted; then because of their young age they will grow into real Canadians and will be a great asset to the province of Quebec and to our country as a whole. I know the refugee children have been accepted into the homes like the real children of the mother and father, and are receiving from each member of the family the deepest affection that the human heart can give to another human being. If the Department of Citizenship and Immigration can conduct a survey as quickly as possible, as I have already said, in order to learn if the refugee children are orphans, it will be in the best interest of the orphans themselves and of the country.
(Translation):
Before resuming my seat, I should like to say a few words in French because I know that the hon. minister understands French very well and speaks it on occasion.
I commend the government and the minister for the manner in which they approached and solved the problem of Hungarian immigration, because they showed a world which is overrun by materialism that Canada has not yet lost its sense of humanity.
If we give those children who have been admitted into this country the same care and attention we give our own, they will be proud to become part of the Canadian community. They will forget the horrors they went through, and that were wrought upon them by people who called themselves their brothers. I therefore trust that those newcomers to Canada will make an important contribution, and that they will prove humanity is still the best law which governs mankind.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the statement made by the minister on this question, which is of particular concern to the Canadian people at this time and in which a great number of people are expressing a keen interest. I realize all the difficulties that surround a crash operation like this. I have discussed the matter with constituents of mine who are supporters of all parties in this house. There has been a particularly lively interest in 
this question in the riding of Kootenay West, and I must say that some of the letters most critical of the policy of the government which have appeared in the local papers were written by some of the most prominent Progressive Conservatives in my constituency, frankly expressing their views and concern about certain aspects of the government's policy in this case. As a result of conversations with people of all parties I agreed to briefly present their views to the house.
I am sure we all agree with the purpose behind this movement. I did not encounter anyone who opposed the coming to Canada of genuine political refugees; in fact, all the people to whom I spoke said they would welcome them. They were concerned, however, about certain aspects of the government's policy. I learned that a good number were concerned that only desirable persons should enter Canada. They were wondering whether the screening of these people was sufficient, and whether there were satisfactory medical examinations. I was very pleased to hear the minister say today that these people were screened and there were adequate medical examinations of those desirous of entering the country.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to interrupt? I would not like a false impression to be created about this matter. These people are in Austria, they are not in Hungary. Austria is part of the free world, and the Austrian government appealed to the rest of the free world to take the refugees as they came and not to select. Great Britain, France and every other European country did just that; and we here as a government, as I announced last November, made a decision to do the same thing. I believe the United States because of its rigid laws does refuse some and leaves them on the doorstep of Austria, but we do not. We give them medical examinations, and if treatment is necessary it is arranged here. We do not reject them for that reason. We are attempting to do as much political screening as is consistent with their rapid movement to Canada.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I thank the minister for his explanation. I realize the difficulties with respect to screening, but on behalf of these constituents I do urge that as time proceeds, every effort be made to see that no unsuitable persons come into this country, that is persons who cannot accept our democratic way of life.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS

CCCLi Charges Canadians Being Replaced by Refugees.

I mention this because that idea has been given to me by a number of people, and I told them I would bring the matter up in the house.
I have just given the minister the views of a good number of people in my constituency, which I promised to do.

Mr. Chairman, I am drawn into this discussion because of one comment made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. He mentioned that there was a variety of opinion concerning this problem of the Hungarian refugees, and he gave honourable mention to the Conservative party.
The problem is one which requires understanding and sympathy, I think, on the part of all members of this house as well as on the part of all citizens of Canada. It is an emergency situation and I feel that it should not be treated from the standpoint of narrow party politics; rather it should be treated from the standpoint of the broad humanitarian viewpoint. It is the first time Canada has attempted to deal with an emergency refugee situation, and there are bound to be many kinds of unanticipated problems.
In my area we have had a small share in the matter and, contrary to the situation which seems to prevail in the constituency of



Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the hon. member for Kootenay West, some of the leading people who have been serving on the voluntary committees are ardent supporters of mine. In the city of Brandon we have had a particularly active group. We have quite successfully coped with the situation, largely because of the generous response on the part of the ordinary citizen.
I would like to commend the officials of the department. There might be some criticism by way of lack of over-all co-ordination by the top levels of the department, but certainly in my contact with Mr. Baillie, Mr. Voisey and Mr. Roberts it has been evident that they have done an excellent job in our particular locality. We are working by trial and error, and I hope the precedents which have been established and the experience which is being acquired will not be forgotten by the department but that they will take advantage to a much greater extent of the opportunity to obtain outstanding citizens by way of immigration emergencies of this kind.
The municipalities are somewhat concerned as to how much of a financial burden arising from this emergency will devolve upon them. There might be some bad eggs among the immigrants, but there are also plenty of good eggs. An immigrant who was being medically examined was found to have several large fragments of shrapnel lodged in his person. He had carried them ever since the days of the fighting in Budapest, and when he was asked why he had not reported the trouble before, even though he was suffering considerable pain, he replied that he was
afraid that if he had he would have been prevented from coming to Canada. That, I think, is typical to a large extent of the spirit of a large proportion of these immigrants. This man has now been hospitalized. Does the department pay the expenses arising from a situation of this kind?

I should like to exempt from this request those refugees who were university students, because it is a well known fact that it was the students of Hungary who were the first of the freedom fighters, and I heartily endorse young men of that type entering our country.
We hope the action of the government on this occasion to obtain suitable immigrants for Canada will be a precedent in obtaining more of the badly needed immigrants from the British Isles. I believe most members of the house would welcome action along similar lines, maybe not at this moment but in the next year or two, to obtain an influx of desirable citizens from the United Kingdom who we understand are very anxious to come to our country in large numbers.
I should like the minister also to inform the house how many newspaper, radio and other personnel were sent to Austria at the expense of the Canadian government, and also what was the exact purpose of sending such personnel there. I endorse what the hon. member for Fort William said to the effect that most of these immigrants are Catholics, and he added that Catholics too can be very hungry. I should like to remind the hon. member for Fort William and the minister that there are millions of people in Asia, especially in India and Hong Kong, who can be very hungry too, and who have been hungry and starving for years. I understand that fully a million in Hong Kong alone are also refugees from communism. Many of them have suffered as severely as many of the refugees whom we are now welcoming to Canada, if not more so.
Then in the displaced persons' camps of West Germany there are still thousands and thousands of refugees from communism, many of whom have suffered equally. Yet in the case of those in Hong Kong, and to a lesser degree in the case of the refugees from communism now in West Germany, we seem to have to pry them past the offices of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in order for them to be able to see the light of day in Canada. Therefore we hope that other refugees from communism will at least be given equally favourable treatment.
