Before the minister replies there are one or two comments I should like to make and questions I should like to ask. First, I should like to express my appreciation of the humanitarian principle which is involved in bringing people from the tribulations of communist domination to the relative freedom of Canada. I believe the people all across Canada appreciate that. Certainly we in this group do, and we would like to see that principle extended to other groups in the world who have suffered from this same domination. If these Hungarians are being brought in on humanitarian grounds I think it would be only right to assume that the government should maintain this principle so far as refugees from Russian domination in other territories of the world are concerned.
Before I deal specifically with that, I should like to ask the minister if consideration will be given to assisting the municipalities which, within a year's time, will be charged with the responsibility of caring for any of these refugees who have not been able to find a place for themselves in Canadian life. It would appear that since the government of Canada has assumed responsibility, and rightly so, for bringing these refugees to Canada, they should continue to shoulder that responsibility rather than letting it fall on the urban and rural municipalities in which these individuals happen to take up residence.
I should like the minister to tell me if the government is giving consideration to affording fairer treatment to the refugees from

communist domination who have settled in Hong Kong. The minister mentioned that some of the Hungarians are now going to be sponsored and will be allowed to come into Canada on that basis. Perhaps the hands of the minister are tied by the platform of the Liberal party adopted in August of 1919, in which section 7 reads:
A more effective restriction of Chinese immigration.
I hope that part of government policy has been changed to one of humanitarian principles, but I doubt that this is so; because I have a case where an individual applied to bring in his adopted son, who is one of the refugees from communist aggression now in Hong Kong, but the minister's humanitarian background has failed to give any recognition to the desirability of this man bringing his remaining child to Canada. I think the minister will be familiar with some of the details. The application has been denied because the minister said it was an adopted child. Surely there are adopted children coming in from Hungary on the same basis. The principle the government has been following of allowing those to come into Canada whom they deemed would fit into the economy is a rather narrow one, especially when they take credit for humanitarian motives.
My plea is that the government be consistent, and if we are going to take credit for being humanitarian then let us prove we are humanitarian by giving consideration to some of those who are suffering the same hardships from communist aggression. It is apparent that the government that has been in office is determined to prevent these people from coming into Canada, as is indicated by their platform of 1919 which evidently is still in force.

There is a book on the press which I hope will be ready in a day or two. I had hoped it would be available a little earlier.
One of the officials of the Department of Labour, who was seconded for a little while to my department by my colleague and who is himself a Hungarian Canadian and the author of a number of important scholarly works, did work out a sort of basic dictionary.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration It appears there is only one printing shop in Canada properly equipped to produce it. I think they were a little congested over the Christmas period and it has taken them a little longer than they had hoped. We hope to get it and other books as quickly as possible. This is a real problem and one you cannot meet very quickly.
As far as education generally goes, of course, we have agreements with practically all the provincial governments except two- maybe it is only one-for sharing the costs of education of adult immigrants. The provincial authorities administer the schemes, and they administer them in most provinces very well indeed. That is particularly true in the province of British Columbia. I think they are working very well to meet this problem, are recognizing its urgency and are coping with it, according to the information I have, very quickly. Certainly that is the general report from most parts of the country.
I do not think the hon. member for Kamloops would mind if we put off debate on whether the refugees should be in camps for longer or shorter periods until my general estimates are before the house. I would like in time to give my reasons for following the policy we are following, but very briefly I would like to say that I spent involuntarily-perhaps that is not true; perhaps voluntarily-two weeks in the hospital, and the day I left, I was reluctant to leave and face the world-

I think there is a terrible danger of people getting this sheltered mentality if they remain too long in comparative idleness in institutions. For my part I believe it is a great deal better to get these people living with Canadian families in the way we live in this country, and I think they will learn far more about the country; they will probably learn far more English far faster. I would like to go on at length on this subject, but I do not think I should.
Both the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Greenwood asked whether I could make any guess as to how many more Hungarians would come into Austria. I cannot; I do not think anybody's guess is worth very much, because we do not know what is going to happen in Hungary. Certainly the number has greatly diminished lately, and I think that is due to the more brutal policies that now appear to be followed by the regime in Hungary.
The question was also raised as to whether we should not have brought the people to

Canada a little faster than we have. Perhaps it would have been possible for us to take one or two thousand more in the months of February and March than we are planning. If the taking of one or two thousand more would have solved the whole problem I think I would have urged my colleagues to do it no matter what difficulties it would have created here, but it would not have solved the whole problem or more than a fringe of it. Having regard to all the circumstances, and having regard to the effort we were making, I felt that since it would not have solved the problem it was better to make these staging arrangements.
I think that with respect to the points raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I have said as much as I need to say. I do not think our real differences are anything like as great as our apparent differences.
I should like once again to thank the hon. member for Red Deer for the very pleasant things he said about my department. In so far as this movement of Hungarians is concerned, they are deserved. These public servants have worked terribly hard. It is not easy to get trained people quickly to handle a greatly increased number of immigrants; and officials must have a certain amount of training if it is to be done at all efficiently. The result was that all of them worked overtime; they gave up practically all of their holidays, and they are still working very hard indeed, both in Europe and all over Canada, and I appreciate what the hon. gentleman said about their service.
I gave the figures a little while ago for the distribution of the Hungarians across the country, and they will appear in Hansard. I gave figures for the ages and the marital status and the breakdown of occupations. I did not read them out, but they will appear in Hansard. The hon. member for Fort William said some very kind things about the local committees in Fort William, and I would like to echo what he said about all these local committees all over this country.
The hon. member for Kamloops said he felt there was not enough co-ordination at the top. I do not think I made myself clear. I do not think we should try to dictate how these things are to be done. We are trying, with our local officials, to do everything we can to co-operate with all those who are interested, and to give all the guidance we are asked to give; but we are not trying to push people around or to boss them unduly. That was really the point I was trying to make. I perhaps did it rather clumsily.
The hon. member for Oxford asked me whether I would elaborate on the movement

of students. I am glad he did, because it gives me an opportunity to express again my great appreciation to the president of the University of Toronto and to a group of businessmen in Toronto who really made the most magnificent arrangements for the reception of this group of students, and I think the whole country should be grateful for what they are doing. I should like to repeat that there is this other group of 100 students who are in Montreal. I hope similar arrangements, perhaps on a less elaborate scale, will be made by interested individuals and corporations and universities, of course, for them.
The hon. member for Oxford raised the question of refunding the transportation expenses of people who had brought out their own relatives. What I said in the house, I am sure all hon. members will recall, was that we intended to cancel the assisted passage loans that had been given up to that time. That was all I said here, and I did not feel it would be proper for us to go beyond what I said here. We will look at these cases. Of course I do not think any case could have arisen after the day I made that statement, so that any of these cases where people borrowed money to pay these passages would' have occurred before the policy was adopted; but if there does seem to be real hardship I will give consideration to what it would be proper for me to ask the taxpayers of Canada generally to do. But it would be quite a sharp departure from anything we have done before to suggest paying people for something they had already decided to do as a matter of family obligation.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska asked me how many of these Hungarians were under the age of nine years. I am afraid I could not answer that offhand. I will try to get the information and give it to him privately. If he refers to children who are not accompanied by their parents the number would be very, very small indeed. I understand the Red Cross have established a tracing service and they are trying to trace information about people who are separated from other members of their families, for the reason given by the hon. gentleman and for other reasons as well.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised some questions, most of which I think I dealt with immediately after he raised them, but there was one about asking these people to repay the passage money. Having announced here that the passage was to be free I do not think we could very well go back on that policy, but I do say this. I have had one or two letters from Hungarians, one very touching, and if it were not so late in the day I would read it. These Hungarians received
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration free passages, and are now voluntarily paying the money back. I do think if those who get good jobs quickly-and some of them are getting very good jobs quickly after they come here

would make a gesture of that kind it would make a very good impression on the Canadian people generally, and would help a great deal to make movements of this kind more acceptable.
A great many of these people, in fact practically all of them, came here with nothing except the clothes they were wearing. During the next few years many of them will have a much more difficult time in establishing themselves than would ordinary immigrants who bring something with them. I think that is and can be the only defence of our policy, and it is the only reason this free transportation is being provided for these people and not for others.

I would imagine that it would certainly not be more than one-third of them, because quite a large number are women and children. Nevertheless a good number actually were fighters, including a large number of the students. I think the reason there are so many single young men is that these are the people, especially the key men, who expected that if they stayed in Hungary they would be deported to Siberia. That is one reason there is a rather large proportion of young men, and another reason is that many of these people had to walk 20 or 30 miles to reach the border of Austria. There were not many widows, aged persons and unaccompanied children, and there are practically no orphans.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration have come, if not to sponsors, to friends. I would like to say a word of special appreciation here for the efforts of the Hungarian Canadians. Everywhere in the country they have done and are doing a wonderful job in assisting us to receive these Hungarian refugees. I think the answer to that question is definitely no. It seems to me that if we are going to have an immigration policy in this country we must bear in mind that we are bringing these people here with a view to their becoming Canadian citizens, and they should be treated like other Canadian citizens. In most localities they cannot qualify for welfare services until after the first year, at which time they can and should qualify just like anybody else in this country, unless we are going to discriminate against one group of residents.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said this vote was not restricted to Hungarians. That is quite true, though all the additional money we are requesting is required because of the Hungarian movement. He did ask me something about the situation in the United Kingdom and what is being done about it. I did say something about that, possibly at a time when the hon. gentleman was unavoidably absent from the chamber, but perhaps I could repeat my remarks.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I have been here all afternoon.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should repeat that as early as last August my department anticipated the need for additional shipping and other forms of transport for the larger movement of immigrants we expected this year, and at the present time we are in active negotiation for a large amount of additional transport. There is no trouble at the present time concerning British immigrants or any


others getting transportation to come to Canada, but there probably will be after the first of April. The ships are not completely booked at the present time, but after the first of April commercial accommodation is not going to be adequate, and we are now taking active steps to get as much transport as we can.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I think the minister misunderstood my question. I was referring to the departmental set-up abroad; for example, in London. I should like to know what is being done to meet the criticism that appeared in the editorial in the Globe and Mail to which I referred.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I have seen the editorials which dealt with transportation, as well as the one to which the hon. gentleman referred. As far as accommodation in London is concerned, it is quite true that when you have an office staff of a size geared to look after from 500 to 700 applicants a day and applicants start coming at the rate of 3,000 a day, as they were when I was in London in December, and as they have been all the time since except on holidays, it is just not possible to deal with everyone who applies on the day he appears. I do not believe anything very serious is lost over this, because the applications are caught up with in a relatively short time, and appointments are made for a later period for those who indicate that in any case they do not intend to come to Canada until several months hence. According to the information that has been given to me, all those who have planned to come to Canada immediately are being dealt with.
We are securing additional accommodation in London. We have opened a new office in Bristol and have increased our accommodation in Glasgow, and are pressing into service just as many officers as we can who are capable of doing the work. I think the problem will be adequately dealt with.
The hon. member for Peel asked me what I knew about "bad eggs". I know nothing at all about the subject, but I am sure that when you bring 10,000 people to a country, as we have already done, without having the time to look them over carefully in the way we try to do with immigrants generally, I do not care what group of 10,000 people you take, you are going to have some who are not going to turn out well.
I do not know very much concerning the details of the incident in Toronto. I read the newspaper accounts and I understand an investigation has been carried out. I have not yet seen the final report of the investigation, but it was quite properly carried out

by the provincial authorities, since it happened in a shelter established by them. It is the only incident about which I have heard.
As to the breakdown of the vote, I have here an approximation, and I hope it will be understood that we do not feel bound to spend it in exactly this way. It is estimated that approximately $2,800,000 will be required for inland transportation in overseas countries to the point of embarkation and for transoceanic transportation, including the costs connected with the removal, embarkation and debarkation of refugees. There is an estimate of approximately $700,000 for inland transportation in Canada. There is also an amount for maintenance, clothing and other expenses incidental to the movement and establishment of Hungarian refugees, including emergency assistance as and when required during the first year in Canada. That is the amount that is expected to be required up to the end of the fiscal year, approximately $390,000.
Then there is an advance of $4,750,000 to the inter-governmental committee on European migration in prepayment of passages over the period. We do not think this is very accurate. It is probably the minimum we expect to need. Then there is an advance of about $300,000 to be paid partly to provincial institutions and to other voluntary organizations for welfare and other assistance and incidental expenses.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: There is one part of the question I asked which I am sure the minister has overlooked inadvertently. I asked if anyone had made any estimate of the total number that might go to Austria. I can understand his answer and am satisfied that perhaps that is not possible. I asked him if it had been possible to make an estimate of the number who might be coming to Canada. Perhaps that could be considered in two ways. First, how many more is it presently envisaged will come if the stream continues to taper off, as it is now doing? Second, has the department made any assessment of the number that it would be feasible for us to take as a result of this refugee movement?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I do not think it would be very sensible for me to attempt to give any estimate. I have given the committee all our commitments, and I think the hon. gentleman has said they add up to something like 27,000 or 28,000. I would certainly anticipate that there would be that number, and that that would be the minimum. How many more it may be possible to take or how many more may want to come by the time it would be possible to arrange it will depend upon a great many factors that are
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration still in doubt, including the question of the shortness of transport which we are bound to face in the summer months. I am quite sure that any estimate I made now would be wrong, and I do not think there would be much profit in making it.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
A related question. The minister has said that as of now no visas had been issued to those who had left Austria and gone to other European countries and the United Kingdom, and that these would not be issued until the flow of those wishing to come directly from Austria had been dealt with, except for sponsored cases. I take it that after the number of refugees coming from Austria has been reduced to manageable proportions, shall we say, visas may then be given to Hungarian refugees who are in other European countries. I should like to know whether that is correct.
In order that we and they may both understand the situation, may I ask if the same arrangement for the payment of passages would apply to those who would then be coming not from Austria but from some other country, which would be considered an intermediate stage in their movement?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I think all these things
should be considered in due course. As far as the 10,000 for whom arrangements have been made with three countries are concerned, their passages will of course be paid. That will also be true of any sponsored cases there may be in any of those European countries. Beyond that, until arrangements are made for other movements I really do not think it would be prudent for me, without consultation with my colleagues, to make any commitments at this stage.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Most of the questions I had intended to ask have been asked already, but there is one specific matter about which I should like to inquire. The suggestion has been made that the Budapest opera company might come to Canada as a group, somewhat as the forestry faculty did, to which reference was made earlier in the discussion. Has the minister any information he could give the committee on that?

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
There were about 1,300
people in the Budapest opera company, and about 200 of those people left Hungary. I imagine that among those would be the more distinguished members of the company. About 100 went almost immediately to other European countries. One or two came to Canada, having relatives in metropolitan Toronto. Some of the group went back to Hungary. Nearly all have gone to one place or another.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Some of them may come to Canada as individuals, but I do not think their coming as a group was ever a serious prospect.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: The minister overlooked two of my questions. I was disappointed that the minister was not able to give a figure as to the number in employment, but I appreciate the difficulties which he pointed out. However, my other two questions I think can be answered. First, I asked the minister a question which I think is of some importance, as to the division of responsibility between the federal and provincial authorities in the finding of employment. Then I asked if there was a plan with regard to giving instruction in English and other necessary things, and whether in fact it is already in effect, to the extent that immigrants are working part of the day in industry and spending another part of the day in obtaining instructions.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
As far as the last question is concerned, I understand that in nearly all cases once these people get employment classes are carried on at night. That is the normal procedure, in order that they may get on with their jobs right away. I dare say there are some who are not employed who may be attending classes in the day time. These classes are all handled by the provincial or local authorities, and I must say that I have not all the details at my fingertips.
The responsibility for finding employment for immigrants is the responsibility of my department. We get the greatest co-operation from the national employment service. It has always been felt that the first placement should be looked after by my department. We have the responsibility of bringing these people here, and it is thought it will make us more responsible about how many we bring.
There is another reason. I think it would be very bad for morale if we had immigrants lining up at employment offices. The employment service does keep us acquainted with vacancies they are not able to fill from their regular lists. They are most co-operative. We have also had excellent co-operation from the provincial governments, but they have no responsibility in the matter.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: In giving me the breakdown of the cost the minister gave the figures for inland, transoceanic and Canadian travel, but he then seemed to repeat by giving the amount covering prepayments for travel.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: The first amount would be spent before the end of the fiscal year, but the other amount covers prepayment for movements after the end of the fiscal year that are presently anticipated.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
In view of the minister's
answer to one of my questions regarding people who have been misled by certain press reports as to what the minister had actually said, I am glad to know that the minister is willing to give instructions that consideration would be given to those cases where people advanced money to friends or to close relatives in order that they might get away from Austria and come to Canada. I think it is most commendable for the minister to have done that.

Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE Payments to municipalities-
540. Grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal properties-Further amount required including authority to make grants under the Municipal Grants Act to the municipalities of Winnipeg, St. James, Edmonton and Vancouver in respect of certain buildings therein notwithstanding that such buildings are located on lands leased by the crown, $2,024,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Would the minister care to give a breakdown of this amount among the four cities named in the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: The breakdown is not complete, for reasons I will come to in a moment. The anticipated expenditure is as follows: Ottawa, $650,000; North York, Ontario, $150,000; Hull, Quebec, $250,000; Halifax, N.S. $150,000; special authority with respect to Winnipeg, St. James, Edmonton and Vancouver, where certain federal properties are on leased lands, $197,000; Calgary, $50,000, and various other centres, $577,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would like to relate that answer more clearly to the item before us. The item refers to $2,024,000 in respect of Winnipeg, St. James, Edmonton and Vancouver-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the item refers to grants under the Municipal Grants Act. The reference to Winnipeg, St. James, Edmonton and Vancouver arises from the fact that in these particular cases the federal properties are situated on non-federal land which did not qualify under the existing provisions of the Municipal Grants Act. We are voting it in this manner to make the position statutory.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: What is the basis for the payments in Vancouver? Is the crown paying the full tax, as though the property were occupied by a private firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The basis for these payments is the existing basis under the 1956-57 statutory provision. The suggested change in the speech from the throne will not be translated into legislation until later in the session.

These are payments on the present basis. In the case of Vancouver the building involved is, I think, a federal building owned by the university; a building which, because it is sited on university property, does not presently qualify.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: The university is not in the city; it cannot be that. The university is on provincial land. Can the minister tell us what buildings in Vancouver are affected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Not at the moment. There is quite a long list, as I recall. This is intended to provide additional funds because municipal corporations, including Vancouver, had put in applications for considerably more than we expected would be the case, and that is why we are short $2 million. In the case of the cities mentioned we are making grants on a basis which has not up to the present been contemplated or provided for in the statute.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I presume these will be occasions when buildings are owned by some private individuals and leased to the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Will these payments, then, be of benefit to the city or to the owner of the property? Will they relieve the owner of the property of paying that much in municipal taxes? I should like to have the names of the buildings in Vancouver to which this applies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I will give that information to the hon. member, but I can assure him that the benefit will accrue to the municipal corporation and not to the lessor.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: I am puzzled by the reference the Minister of Finance has made to a building located on property belonging to the University of British Columbia-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Perhaps what you understood me to say was that because these buildings are not situated on federally owned property they are not covered by the present provisions of the act, and this is a way of covering them so that grants can be made in respect of them to municipal corporations.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Are they buildings on which taxes are not being paid now by the private owners?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
These, as I understand it, are buildings that are on property leased to the federal government, I thought by the university, but if the hon. member from Van-couver-Quadra corrects me I must admit I am wrong. At any rate, I think it is provincial or university property which is not taxable by the municipal corporation. Therefore we are taking this way of making it
Supply-Finance
subject to our generosity, if you like to call it that, under the Municipal Grants Act.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Is there anything in the situation that did not exist before? Were these buildings formerly not owned by the government? The change that has taken place I understand is a change in the percentage that has been applied. This seems to be a change affecting certain buildings.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The change that has been made is this. We have decided to pay with regard to certain buildings in these particular cities, on which up to the moment we have not paid. There is no change with regard to the character of the buildings or the leasehold property. It was decided we ought to pay on these particular buildings, and we are asking parliament for authority to do so.
Mr. Pallet!: A series of other municipalities have been mentioned. Is this additional payment a payment on new construction, or does it represent extra grants on previous submissions by municipalities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: As I said, the number of applications from our municipal corporations has grown; there were a great many more than we had anticipated, and the sum of half a million dollars which I referred to covers a number of municipal corporations in regard to which we had no idea we might have to make grants. In other cases the grants are for greater sums of money, with the result that the estimate I placed before parliament last spring has proved inadequate. I have not with me the long list of all the additional corporations that would be covered; I think I gave information about that in the spring when the amendment was put through, but I can assure members of this committee that the amount of money we have had to pay in the meantime has surprised us.

maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: Is this a case where the conscience of the department has become more active than it was before, and they therefore feel they should pay on leased premises?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REFERENCE BY MR. SPEAKER TO ASKING OF QUESTIONS
speechtext: As a Baptist to a Presbyterian I suggest we should not discuss consciences, because sometimes we do not agree.

Item agreed to.
University grants-
541. To authorize payments to the national conference of Canadian universities (hereinafter called "the conference") for the purpose of making grants to institutions of higher learning in accordance with an agreement entered into or to be entered into, with the approval of the governor in council, between the Minister of Finance and the conference, such agreement to include, inter alia, provision that the total amount of grants to all the institutions of higher learning in any one province be calculated by multiplying the population of the province by $1, and that any amount payable to

Supply-Finance

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is a situation here which I do not fully understand.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Monday, of course, is private members' day, and I would not suggest that we would not take the full day. On the other hand, on one previous occasion we
found that we did not and I had not announced government business. Therefore on Monday, should private members' business be exhausted and government orders reached, we shall proceed with the Canada Council legislation and the Canadian wheat board bill. On Tuesday we shall take the same legislation, together with the other items on the order paper, and on Wednesday the same. On Thursday, which is private members' day again, we shall follow the same procedure.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Dissolve on Friday.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: What about these supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: We will have to reach them by Friday next. Frankly I had hoped we could pass them today. I hope my last remark, Mr. Speaker, did not indicate a lack of thanks for the co-operation I have had in the last hour.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
